The blocks that have contiguous reads (multiple threads reading at the same time) are shown in boldface. Note that multiple threads can read, but only one thread can write at a time.

### 16.5\. Interlocked Operations

Many processors support certain operations that are guaranteed by the runtime not to be interrupted. These operations are useful when you're dealing with threads, because you can use them without using locking. In the CLR these operations are encapsulated in the `Interlocked` class. This class exposes the `Increment()`, `Decrement()`, `Exchange()`, and `Compare Exchange()` methods, which can be used on the `long` and `int` data types.

In [Listing 16.16](#0672324024_ch16lev1sec4.html_ch16list16), the `Interlocked.Decrement` operation is used to decrement the number of threads accessed in a thread-safe manner. The runtime guarantees that the interlocked decrement operation will not be interrupted.

You should use interlocked operations to improve performance, and avoid the use of trivial locks for basic operations such as incrementing and decrementing `int` and `long` data types. For example, we could make [Listing 16.13](#0672324024_ch16lev1sec4.html_ch16list13) instantly thread-safe by using the `Interlocked` increment and decrement operations in the `add()` and `remove()` methods.

### 16.6\. Summary

Thread-related classes and delegates are defined in the `System.Threading` namespace. The four ways to create threads in C# are as follows:

1.  Manually creating threads. This approach gives the most flexibility because the creator of the thread can control the thread's attributes. This approach is also how Java programmers create threads. But because the onus of managing the life cycle of the thread is on the programmer, this approach of creating threads should be avoided if possible. Improperly managing the life of the thread could cannibalize system resources.

2.  Using the `System.Threading.ThreadPool` class. This is the recommended approach to creating threads because it exploits the system-specified `ThreadPool` class, which takes care of managing the life cycle of the created threads.

3.  Using the `System.Threading.Timer` class. This is the recommended approach for creating threads that execute a task periodically.

4.  Using the asynchronous callback mechanism. Although this approach does not directly create a thread, it simulates asynchronous behavior and provides a generic mechanism for information sharing between the caller thread and the execution thread.

In most cases, you can synchronize threads by using the `lock` keyword, which is similar to Java's `synchronized` keyword. To obtain finer control over the synchronization blocks, C# provides the `Monitor` class. C# provides `ReaderWriterLock`s, which are useful for a typical programming problem of multiple threads trying to read an object and only one thread trying to write to it. The C# `Interlocked` class provides operations that can be executed on the `int` and `long` data types. These operations cannot be interrupted; they are atomic and therefore preclude the need for specifying locks for trivial tasks.

## Chapter 17\. Using C# Properties, Indexers, and Attributes

In the past few chapters we have seen how similar C# is to Java in many aspects. The makers of C# have introduced quite a few new concepts in C# that are very critical to writing good C# code. A Java programmer might be tempted to write C# code using Java conventions, and that is fine, but you might carry over the inefficiencies of Java into the C# code. The constructs that we discuss in this chapter are specifically designed to address these inefficiencies. Three constructs—properties, indexers, and attributes—have no Java equivalents.

### 17.1\. Properties

An object's attributes can be accessed directly (if they are declared `public`) or through `get` and `set` methods (accessors and mutators). These methods provide a single point of access to the attributes. You can change the implementation of these methods without affecting the code that calls them. C# provides the property construct, which makes the calling of these `get` and `set` methods transparent to the end user.

A property is typically used to model simple attributes. For example, you can set or get the color of a car (an object) using both properties and methods, as shown next. Using properties:

```
 1) car.Color = "red";
2) string color = car.Color;
```

Using method calls:

```
 3) car.SetColor ("red");
4) string color = car.GetColor();
```

The property syntax is more readable. In line 1, setting the `Color` property actually calls a setter inside the `car` object without the end user having to know about it. Similarly, in line 2 you call the getter implicitly merely by retrieving the property and assigning it to a variable.

Let's look at an example. [Listing 17.1](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec1.html_ch17list01) shows a `Student` class with various properties defined.

##### Listing 17.1\. A `Student` Class with Three Properties (C#)

|  
```
 using System;

public class Student {

  int size;
  int count;
  string name;
  string id;

  public int Count {
    get {
      return Int32.Parse("te4t");
    }
    set {
      count = value;
    }
  }
  public string ID {
    get {
      return id;
    }
    set {
      id = value;
    }
  }
  public string Name {
    get {
      return name;
    }
  }
  public int Size {
    get {
      if (size == 1) calcSize();
      return size;
    }
    set {
      size = value;
      calcCount();
    }
  }
  private void calcSize() {
    //Do something with the size here.
  }
  private void calcCount() {
    //Do something with the count here.
  }

  public static void Main(string[] args) {

    Student s = new Student();
    Console.WriteLine("Name ="+(s.Name == null));
    s.Count = 2;
    try {
      Console.WriteLine(s.Count);
    } catch (Exception e) {
      Console.WriteLine(e.Message);
    }
    s.ID = "Test";
  }
}
```

 |

The output of [Listing 17.1](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec1.html_ch17list01) is as follows:

```
 Name =True
Input string was not in a correct format.
```

In [Listing 17.1](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec1.html_ch17list01), the `ID` property is a simple property with both the `get{}` and `set{}` blocks defined. Note that in the `set{}` block, the term `value` is a C# keyword. The `value` keyword should be assigned to the attribute being wrapped by the property. The CLR is smart enough to resolve the type of the attribute to which the `value` keyword is assigned, so you don't have to do any type conversion in the `set{}` block. The `get{}` block merely returns the value of the `id` attribute. The `ID` property is a simple property that wraps the `id` attribute. External code can get or set the value of the attribute `id` by working on the `ID` property. Note that both the `get` and `set` locks have the same access modifier (`public`).

The `Size` property wraps access to the `size` attribute. The `get{}` and `set{}` blocks for this property involve some extra processing. This is perfectly legal. Remember that the `get{}` and `set{}` blocks are like getter and setter methods. Fortunately, the processing in the `get{}` and `set{}` blocks consists of dummy method calls. In reality, the processing can be anything from trivial in-memory operations to database access.

As you can see, the simplicity of setting and getting a property can wrap a lot of complex, behind-the-scenes operations that the user is totally unaware of. Although a property is meant to simplify syntax, a property that hides CPU- and memory-intensive operations can be wrongfully used in a manner that could affect performance. For example, in the following snippet, `Balance` and `Interest` are both properties of the `account` object, and both can access the database:

```
 for (i =0; i < 100000; ++i) {
  sum += account.Balance + account.Interest;
}
```

Although the syntax looks simple, going to the database 100,000 times in a loop can result in poor performance.

The `Name` property wraps access to the `name` attribute. The `Name` property does not have a `set{}` block. This makes the property read-only. This is similar to a Java class having only an accessor for an attribute. When you print the `Name` property for a `student`, its value is `null`. However, unlike Java, the word “null” is not printed to the console; instead, a blank space is printed (not shown in the output).

The `Count` property wraps access to the `count` attribute. The `Count` property will throw a `Parsing` exception in the `get{}` block because it is trying to parse an alphanumeric text to an `int`. Unfortunately, the fact that there is an exception being thrown is not indicated anywhere in the signature of the property. Because C# does not have a `throws` clause, the user of the property has no way to know which exceptions must be accounted for in using that property.

Visual Basic programmers envisage properties as simple wrappers over attributes of objects, such as `Color`, `Width`, and `Height`. In fact, that was the motivation behind the C# property construct. However, the flexibility of overriding the `get{}` and `set{}` blocks with custom code can be abused. You should never put complex CPU- and memory-intensive code in the `get{}` and `set{}` blocks of a property. Properties should be thought of as simple wrappers to the object's attributes.

In [Listing 17.1](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec1.html_ch17list01), all the `get{}` and `set{}` blocks had the same access modifier. This is where properties are less flexible than methods. You can change the access modifier of a setter or getter method, but a `public` property will lead to `public get{}` and `set{}` blocks.

[Listing 17.2](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec1.html_ch17list02) shows that, like member functions, properties can also be declared using `virtual`, `override`, or `abstract` modifiers. These modifiers are placed on the property and affect both the getter and the setter. When a derived class declares a property with the same name as in the base class, it hides the entire property; it is not possible to hide only the getter or the setter. Properties can also be `static`. `Static` properties are just like member methods in that they cannot be declared with the `virtual`, `abstract`, or `override` modifier. [Listing 17.2](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec1.html_ch17list02) shows an `abstract` property, `Area`, of the `Graphic` object, which is overridden by the `Area` property of the `Circle` class.

##### Listing 17.2\. A Simple Abstract Property (C#)

|  
```
 using System;

public abstract class Graphic {

  public abstract double Area {
    get;
    set;
  }
}

class Circle : Graphic {
  double area = 1;
  double radius;
  public Circle(double rad) { radius = rad; }

  public override double Area {
    get {
      if (area == 1) {
        area = Math.PI * Math.Pow(radius,2);
      }
      return area;
    }
    set {
      area = value;
      radius = Math.Sqrt((area/Math.PI));
    }
  }

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    Graphic g = new Circle(5.6);
    Console.WriteLine(g.Area);
  }
}
```

 |

The output of [Listing 17.2](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec1.html_ch17list02) is as follows:

```
 98.5203456165759
```

In sum, here are the pros and cons of the C# property construct. Pros:

*   It has simplified syntax.

*   You do not have to be aware of the method signature to use it.

*   A property can throw an exception without a caller having to know about that exception.

Cons:

*   Because properties are deceptively simple, they are most likely to be used as regular variables in operations or in loops. Care should be taken that a property does not hide CPU- and memory-intensive operations in its `get{}` and `set{}` blocks.

*   A property forces the same access modifier on the `get{}` and `set{}` blocks.

### 17.2\. Indexers

Arrays provide a convenient way to get and set a value of an element. Indexers allow a list of ordinary objects to be accessed as though they were arrays. Just as a property looks like a field but has methods to perform get and set operations, an indexer looks like an array but has methods to perform array indexing operations.

#### 17.2.1\. Indexers with an Integer Index

The class in [Listing 17.3](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec2.html_ch17list03) shows an indexer with an integer index. The indexer is specified using `this[..]` syntax. The indexer has `get` and `set` blocks. If you remove the `set` block, the indexer becomes read-only. The return type is `object`, and again the keyword `value` appears in the `set` block. The index of the indexer is specified as the argument of `this[..]`.

[Listing 17.3](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec2.html_ch17list03) shows how any custom object can define an indexer and can be treated as an array.

##### Listing 17.3\. An Indexer with an Integer as an Index (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Collections;

public class Rows {

  ArrayList list;
  public Rows(ArrayList param) {
    list = new ArrayList(param);
  }

  public object this[int index] {
    get
    {
      return list[index];
    }
    set
    {
      list[index] = value;
    }
  }
  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    ArrayList list = new ArrayList();
    list.Add(2);
    list.Add(245);
    list.Add(44);
    Rows rows = new Rows(list);
    for (int i =0; i < list.Count; ++i)
      Console.WriteLine(rows [i]);
  }
}
```

 |

The output of [Listing 17.3](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec2.html_ch17list03) is as follows:

```
 2
245
44
```

In [Listing 17.3](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec2.html_ch17list03) the indexer is specified by the following lines:

```
 public object this[int index] {
  get
  {
    return list[index];
  }
  set
  {
    list[index] = value;
  }
}
```

It is an integer-based index because the index is declared as an `int`. Essentially, we know that an `ArrayList` defines an indexer that makes it possible to access it like an array. The `Rows` class wraps an `ArrayList` and also wraps the indexer functionality of the `ArrayList`. The `Rows` class merely delegates the indexer calls to the underlying `ArrayList` object.

#### 17.2.2\. Indexers with a String Index

Unlike arrays, an indexer index can be a string. [Listing 17.4](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec2.html_ch17list04) shows an indexer with a string index. The string index is maintained as a `Hashtable`, and the two indices retrieve their data from different sources. The integerbased index gets data from an `ArrayList`, and the string-based index gets data from a `Hashtable`.

##### Listing 17.4\. Indexer with String Index (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Collections;

public class RGBColorCodes {

  Hashtable table;
  public RGBColorCodes() {
    table = new Hashtable();
  }
  public void Add(object key, object val) {
    table.Add(key, val);
  }

  public object this[string key] {
    get {
      return table[key];
    }
    set {
      table[key] = value;
    }
  }
  public int Count {
    get {
      return table.Count;
    }
  }

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    RGBColorCodes codes = new RGBColorCodes();
    codes.Add("maroon","800000");
    codes.Add("darkred","8B0000");
    codes.Add("deeppink","FF1493");
    codes.Add("mediumpurple","9370DB");
    codes.Add("springgreen","00FF7F");
    codes.Add("lavenderblush","FFF0F5");
    Console.WriteLine(codes["springgreen"]);
  }
}
```

 |

Here is the output of [Listing 17.4](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec2.html_ch17list04):

```
 00FF7F
```

The `RGBColorCodes` class stores RGB color codes and their names in a `Hashtable`, which is indexed by the color name. You can obtain the color code of a particular color using the indexer notation. The indexer is defined in the listing using the following lines:

```
 public object this[string key] {
  get {
    return table[key];
  }
  set {
    table[key] = value;
  }
}
```

Note that in both [Listing 17.3](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec2.html_ch17list03) and [Listing 17.4](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec2.html_ch17list04), the `get{}` and `set{}` block implementations are trivial; in reality, they could be more complex. Again, you should be careful in not hiding complex CPU- or memory-intensive operations inside these blocks. The indexer notation is most likely to be used in the context of a loop, and having CPU-intensive implementations in the `get{}` and `set{}` blocks of the indexer will slow the iteration.

#### 17.2.3\. Indexers with Multiple Indices

Indexers simplify the API. Consider a convoluted data structure such as a `Hashtable` of `ArrayList`s. Let's say this structure is used to store database rows so that the primary key is stored as the `Hashtable` key and the values of the columns are stored in the `ArrayList`. To access a column of this dataset based on the primary key or hash table key, you have the option of the following sample method calls (of course, you can get arcane in your method signatures if you want to):

```
 Dataset.GetRow(int row).GetColumn(int col);
Dataset.GetData(int row, int column);
```

You would also have to provide the setter methods. You could replace the preceding mess using one indexer:

```
 DataSet[int row, int column]
```

Chess and checkers players will immediately appreciate this indexer notation. In fact, a dataset is essentially a table, so why not make it accessible as a table structure? [Listing 17.5](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec2.html_ch17list05) shows a `DataSet` object with multiple indexers. Notice that in the `Main` method, the client calls to the `get` and `set` objects in the `DataSet` have been simplified.

##### Listing 17.5\. Indexer with Multiple Indices (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Collections;

public class DataSet {

  ArrayList list;
  Hashtable table;

  public DataSet() {
    table = new Hashtable();
    LoadData() {
  }

  private void LoadData(){
    table.Add(1, GenerateList(1));
    table.Add(2, GenerateList(2));
    table.Add(3, GenerateList(3));
    table.Add(4, GenerateList(4));
  }

  private ArrayList GenerateList(int j) {
    ArrayList list = new ArrayList();
    for (int i =0; i < j; ++i) {
      list.Add(i);
    }
    return list;
  }

  public object this[int row, int column] {
    get {
      return ((ArrayList) table[row])[column];
    }
    set {
      ((ArrayList) table[row])[column] = value;
    }
  }

  public void print() {
    foreach (object o in table.Keys) {
      ArrayList list = (ArrayList) table[o];
      Console.WriteLine("Key {0} has the following values ", o);
      for (int i =0 ; i < list.Count; ++i) {
        Console.WriteLine(list[i]);
      }
    }
  }

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    DataSet ds = new DataSet();
    ds.print();
    ds[2,0] = 3;
    ds.print();
  }
}
```

 |

The output of [Listing 17.5](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec2.html_ch17list05) is as follows:

```
 Key 4 has the following values
0
1
2
3
Key 3 has the following values
0
1
2
Key 2 has the following values
0
1
Key 1 has the following values
0
Key 4 has the following values
0
1
2
3
Key 3 has the following values
0
1
2
Key 2 has the following values
3
1
Key 1 has the following values
0
```

In [Listing 17.5](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec2.html_ch17list05) the indexer is defined using the following lines:

```
 public object this[int row, int column] {
    get {
      return ((ArrayList) table[row])[column];
     }
    set {
      ((ArrayList) table[row])[column] = value;
    }
  }
```

Indexers with multiple indices give you the freedom to represent the access to data in whatever form is most relevant to the problem domain being addressed. For example, a chess square could be referred to as `chessboard [row`, `column]`, as opposed to `chessboard.getRow().getColumn()`. Such indexers can trim the code and make it more intuitive and readable.

### 17.3\. Attributes

Modern programming languages often use declarative constructs to change the runtime behavior of the program. These constructs often exist in property files, `.ini` files, or configuration files. The Enterprise JavaBeans specification of Java uses declarative syntax to define the transactional behavior of the EJB. The standard policy file that ships with the JDK distribution contains security-related declarative constructs that dictate which Java classes get which permissions at runtime.

The C# language provides the `System.Attribute` class, which is used to model a declarative construct. Java does not have a first-class object for modeling declarative constructs. C# attributes can be used in the source code on specific code elements such as methods, classes, constructors, and assemblies. These are annotations that can be used to change or define the runtime behavior of the object. They have an API, and so you can programmatically access the attributes defined on an object. By judiciously defining the attributes, you can get very granular and specific with the runtime behavior.

By placing the attribute on a specific code element, you inherently define the scope at which the attribute will apply. Code elements to which attributes apply are often called targets and typically include the following: `Assembly`, `Module`, `Class`, `Struct`, `Enum`, `Constructor`, `Method`, `Property`, `Field`, `Event`, `Interface`, `Parameter`, `ReturnValue`, `Delegate`, `All`, and `ClassMembers`. You specify attributes by placing the name of the attribute and enclosing it in square brackets in front of the code element where it applies. For example, `[DllImport]` is a standard attribute that can be placed in front of a method:

```
 [DllImport] public class WindowsFileReader{. . . }
```

Attributes can have parameters:

```
 [DllImport("user32.dll", SetLastError=false, ExactSpelling=false)]
```

Attribute parameters can be of the following types:

*   `Bool`

*   `Byte`

*   `Char`

*   `Double`

*   `Float`

*   `Int`

*   `Long`

*   `Short`

*   `String`

*   `Object`

*   `System.Type`

*   A `public enum`

*   A one-dimensional array of any of these types

More than one attribute can be placed in front of a code element, and an attribute can be used multiple times on different code elements. These are called multiuse attributes. In certain situations, the target of an attribute (that is, the code element to which the attribute applies) appears to be ambiguous. For example, in the following method declaration, the `SomeAttr` attribute could apply to the method or to the method's return value:

```
 [SomeAttr] int Method1( string s )
```

To resolve the ambiguity, C# has a set of default targets for each kind of declaration. You can override these default targets by explicitly specifying attribute targets:

```
 [method: SomeAttr] int Method1( string s ) // applies to method
[return: SomeAttr] int Method1( string s ) // applies to return
                                                           value
[SomeAttr] int Method1( string s ) // default: applies to method
```

[Table 17.1](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec3.html_ch17table01) lists all declarations in which attributes are allowed; for each declaration, the possible targets for attributes on the declaration are listed in the second column.

Attributes whose target is the assembly or the module are considered global attributes. The `CLSCompliant` attribute indicates whether all types defined in the assembly comply with the .NET Framework Common Language Specification:

```
 [assembly: System.CLSCompliant(true)]
```

Table 17.1\. Declaration List

| Declaration | Possible Targets |
| --- | --- |
| Assembly | assembly |
| Module | module |
| Class | type |
| Struct | type |
| Interface | type |
| Enum | type |
| Delegate | type, return |
| Method | method, return |
| Parameter | param |
| Field | field |
| Property—indexer | property |
| Property—get accessor | method, return |
| Property—set accessor | method, param, return |
| Event—field | event, field, method |
| Event—property | event, property |
| Event—add | method, param |
| Event—remove | method, param |

For the most part, we will be dealing with the predefined attributes in the .NET environment. However, you can define custom attributes. To define an attribute you extend the `System.Attribute` class. It's good to name your custom attribute class with the `Attribute` suffix after the class name so that it is easy to identify as an attribute class.

An attribute class is like a regular class except that there is a predefined attribute called `[AttributeUsage]` that your custom attribute must specify over its class. This defines the ways in which your custom attribute will be used. The `[AttributeUsage]` attribute is a single-use attribute. `[AttributeUsage]` is also an alias for `System.AttributeUsageAttribute`. The syntax of the `[AttributeUsage]` attribute is

```
 [AttributeUsage(target,
AllowMultiple=allowmultiple,Inherited=inherited)]
```

where `target` specifies the language element on which the attribute can be placed. A `true` value for `AllowMultiple` means that the attribute is multiuse. A `true` value for `Inherited` means that the attribute is inherited by derived classes.

[Listing 17.6](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec3.html_ch17list06) shows a custom `Modified` attribute that you can place on a class to indicate when the class was modified and by whom. A source-control program such as CVS or Visual SourceSafe easily keeps track of all this information. However, if you want to do this programmatically, you can do it in C#. The `ClassModifiedAttribute` takes one argument (`modifiedby`). The attribute can be used multiple times on the class, and also its sole target is a class. The attribute is then used on a custom class called `Algorithm`. Using reflection, you can get the custom attributes defined on a class and have the values of attributes printed. [Listing 17.6](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec3.html_ch17list06) allows you to collect historical data about when the class was modified.

##### Listing 17.6\. Custom Attributes (C#)

|  
```
 using System;

[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class, AllowMultiplerue)]
class ClassModifiedAttribute : Attribute {
  System.DateTime date;
  string modifiedBy;
  public ClassModifiedAttribute (string modifiedBy) {
    date = System.DateTime.Now;
    this.modifiedBy = modifiedBy;
  }
  public string ModifiedBy {
    get {
      return this.modifiedBy;
    }
  }
  public System.DateTime ModifiedDate {
    get {
      return this.date;
    }
  }
  public override string ToString() {
    return "The class was modified by "+ modifiedBy +" on "+
                                                             date;
  }
}
[ClassModified ("John")]
[ClassModified ("Damien")]
[ClassModified ("Jack")]
class Algorithm {
  public static void Main (string[] args) {
      Type type = typeof (Algorithm);
    foreach (ClassModifiedAttribute att in
    type.GetCustomAttributes(
              typeof(ClassModifiedAttribute),false)) {
      Console.WriteLine ("Class was modified by "+att.ModifiedBy + " on " +att.ModifiedDate);
    }
  }
}
```

 |

The output of [Listing 17.6](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec3.html_ch17list06) is as follows:

```
 Class was modified by Damien on 11/2/2002 7:33:53 PM
Class was modified by Jack on 11/2/2002 7:33:53 PM
Class was modified by John on 11/2/2002 7:33:53 PM
```

Looking at the output you will quickly recognize a problem with this attribute. Because you are setting the date to `System.DateTime.Now`, every time you try to get the history, it gives you the current time when the program was run instead of the true date when the class was modified. To fix this, we change the attribute to take a string date, which the modifier of the class specifies. The modified code is shown in [Listing 17.7](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec3.html_ch17list07).

##### Listing 17.7\. Modified `ClassModified` Custom Attribute (C#)

|  
```
 using System;

[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class, AllowMultiplerue)]
class ClassModifiedAttribute : Attribute {
  string date;
  string modifiedBy;
  public ClassModifiedAttribute (string modifiedBy, string date ) {
    this.date = date;
    this.modifiedBy = modifiedBy;
  }
  public string ModifiedBy {
    get {
      return this.modifiedBy;
    }
  }
  public string ModifiedDate {
    get {
      return this.date;
    }
  }
  public override string ToString() {
    return "The class was modified by "+ modifiedBy +" on "+
                                                             date;
  }
}

[ClassModified ("John", "2/5/2002")]
[ClassModified ("Damien", "3/6/2002")]
[ClassModified ("Jack", "4/7/2002")]
class Algorithm {
  public static void Main (string[] args) {
    Type type = typeof (Algorithm);
    foreach (ClassModifiedAttribute att in
             type.GetCustomAttributes(
                  typeof(ClassModifiedAttribute),false)) {
      Console.WriteLine ("Class was modified by "+
                att.ModifiedBy + " on " +att.ModifiedDate);
    }
  }
}
```

 |

The output of [Listing 17.7](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec3.html_ch17list07) is as follows:

```
 Class was modified by Damien on 3/6/2002
Class was modified by Jack on 4/7/2002
Class was modified by John on 2/5/2002
```

The class is now fixed to show the correct historical data.

### 17.4\. Summary

C# has three programming constructs that do not have direct equivalents in the Java world: properties, indexers, and attributes.

Properties are a façade for an object's attributes or fields. Properties provide `get{}` and `set{}` blocks, which are like the accessor and mutator methods. The code in the `get{}` and `set{}` blocks is called by the runtime transparently whenever the user of the property sets or gets the value of the property. Properties have the pros and cons shown in [Table 17.2](#0672324024_ch17lev1sec4.html_ch17table02).

You should use properties only for wrapping the fields of an object so that the `get` and `set` blocks do minimal or no processing in getting and setting the value of the property.

Indexers let you use array-like notation to access a collection of objects. Indexers can be integer- or string-based. A single object can define multiple indexers, and an indexer can be defined with multiple indices. Indexers have the same pros and cons as properties. They simplify the overall look and feel of the code, but if there is CPU- or memory-intensive code in the underlying `get{}` and `set{}` blocks, then it could negatively affect the performance of the application depending on how the indexer is used. It is recommended that indexers be used when the `get` and `set` blocks of the indexer do minimal or no processing.

Table 17.2\. Pros and Cons of C# Properties

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Simplify syntax. Properties can be get or set like ordinary programming variables, thereby simplifying the overall look and feel of the code.Properties do not require the user of the property to know anything about the property signature because there is none. | Properties simplify syntax by hiding the calls to the code in the `get{}` and `set{}` blocks. Placing any CPU- or memory-intensive code in these blocks could result in poor performance of the resulting application depending on how the property is being used.Properties do not throw any exceptions, and so the user does not know beforehand which exceptions to look out for when using a property.Properties do not allow for different access modifiers on the `get{}` and `set{}` blocks. |

Attributes provide a declarative way to dynamically change the behavior of code at runtime. The `System.Attribute` class also provides an API to programmatically access and change the attribute. Associated with every C# object there is metadata (information about the methods, fields, interfaces, types), and attributes allow you to extend that metadata.

## Chapter 18\. Delegates and Event Programming

This chapter explores one of the new constructs of C# that has no equivalent in the Java programming language. C#'s language API is peppered with uses of this construct. If you examine the threading and I/O APIs, you'll find that the entire asynchronous callback mechanism is based on this new construct, which is called delegates.

Another reason for the support of delegates in C# concerns function pointers, which have been a popular construct in C++ and C but are not supported in Java. Because Java treats everything as a class, the makers of Java did not find the need for a separate construct for function pointers. C#, however, was not meant to lure only Java programmers. C#'s delegates make C and C++ programmers feel at home. Delegates are essentially references to a function (instead of an object) that can be called. Just like a regular object reference, this reference to a function can be an instance reference, static, or a property.

### 18.1\. Using Delegates

[Listing 18.1](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec1.html_ch18list01) shows a simple delegate.

##### Listing 18.1\. A Simple Delegate Example (C#)

|  
```
 1 using System;
2 public class Test {
3   public delegate float CalcIncome(float hourlyWages);
4   public static void Main(string[] args) {
      CalcIncome del = new
      CalcIncome(Person.CalcAnnualIncome);
      Console.WriteLine(del(26));
5   }
6   public class Person {
7   public float income;
8   public static float CalcMonthlyIncome(float hourlyWages) {
      return hourlyWages * 160;
9   }
10  public static float CalcAnnualIncome(float hourlyWages) {
        resturn hourlyWages * 160 * 12;
11  }
12}
```

 |

The first step is to declare the delegate, which is done in line 3:

```
 public delegate float CalcIncome(float hourlyWages);
```

This declares a public delegate called `CalcIncome` that takes a `float` as a parameter and returns a `float` as a result.

The entry point instantiates the delegate using the following line:

```
 CalcIncome del = new CalcIncome(Person.CalcAnnualIncome);
```

Note that when you instantiate a delegate you must essentially pass the name of the function that matches the signature of the delegate—that is, the name of the function that will actually get called after the delegate is activated. A delegate is like a function pointer; in the preceding line we are simply getting a reference `del` to a function pointer pointing to the function `Person.CalcAnnualIncome`. This function can be any function as long as its signature matches that of the delegate (takes a `float` and returns a `float`). The `Person.CalcAnnualIncome` and `Person.CalcMonthlyIncome` methods are both defined in a separate `Person` class. Note that these two methods do not have to be `static`.

The following line invokes the delegate:

```
 Console.WriteLine(del(26));
```

Essentially the runtime passes the argument `26` to the actual function wrapped by our delegate `del`, which is `Person.CalcAnnualIncome`, and then calls that method. This returns the value, which is then printed as `49920`.

This is the gist of delegates.

At this point you may wonder how delegates handle exceptions thrown by the underlying method they are pointing to. [Listing 18.2](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec1.html_ch18list02) answers that question.

##### Listing 18.2\. Exception Handling in Delegates (C#)

|  
```
 using System;

public class Test {

  public delegate float CalcIncome(string hourlyWages);

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    CalcIncome del = new CalcIncome(Person.CalcAnnualIncome);
    Console.WriteLine(del("hghg"));
  }
}

public class Person {

  public float income;
  public static float CalcMonthlyIncome(string hourlyWages) {
    return (float) Double.Parse(hourlyWages) * 160;
  }
  public static float CalcAnnualIncome(string hourlyWages) {
    return (float) Double.Parse(hourlyWages) * 160 * 12;
  }
}
```

 |

In [Listing 18.2](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec1.html_ch18list02) the delegate is modified to accept a string instead of a float as a parameter. Passing an invalid numeric string causes a `System.FormatException`, which is then thrown by the CLR.

Delegates can be packaged as properties or `static` members of a class. In the previous listings the delegate was an instance member of the `Test` class. [Listing 18.3](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec1.html_ch18list03) shows delegates as `static` read-only members of the `Test` class.

##### Listing 18.3\. Delegates as `static` Members (C#)

|  
```
 using System;

public class Test {

  public delegate float CalcIncome(float hourlyWages);

  public static readonly CalcIncome MonthlyIncome = new
                          CalcIncome(Person.CalcMonthlyIncome);

  public static readonly CalcIncome AnnualIncome = new
                           CalcIncome(Person.CalcAnnualIncome);

  public static void Main(string[] args) {

    try {
      Console.WriteLine(Test.MonthlyIncome(40));
      Console.WriteLine(Test.AnnualIncome(40));
    } catch(Exception e) {
      Console.WriteLine(e.StackTrace);
    }
  }
}

public class Person {

  public float income;

  public static float CalcMonthlyIncome(float hourlyWages) {
    return hourlyWages * 160;
  }
  public static float CalcAnnualIncome(float hourlyWages) {
    return hourlyWages * 160 * 12;
  }
}
```

 |

In [Listing 18.3](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec1.html_ch18list03), the delegates are created as two `static` members (`MonthlyIncome` and `AnnualIncome`), and these are invoked.

### 18.2\. Multicasting

So far we have seen that delegates encapsulate a single function call. However, a delegate can also refer to multiple functions. Just as an object method call can encapsulate multiple method calls within it, a delegate can actually call multiple functions.

You can use the operators “+” and “-” to add and remove delegates. Whenever a delegate points to multiple functions, all the functions get called in the order in which they are added to the invocation list. The invocation list is a CLR-maintained list of functions of a delegate that need to get called.

[Listing 18.4](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec2.html_ch18list04) shows a delegate pointing to multiple function calls.

##### Listing 18.4\. Adding Delegates (C#)

|  
```
 using System;

public class Test {

  public delegate float CalcIncome(float hourlyWages);

  public static readonly CalcIncome MonthlyIncome = new
                          CalcIncome(Person.CalcMonthlyIncome);

  public static readonly CalcIncome AnnualIncome = new
                           CalcIncome(Person.CalcAnnualIncome);

  public static readonly CalcIncome AllIncomes = MonthlyIncome
                                                 + AnnualIncome;

  public static void Main(string[] args) {

    try {
      Console.WriteLine(Test.AllIncomes(40));
    } catch(Exception e) {
      Console.WriteLine(e.StackTrace);
    }
  }
}

public class Person {

  public float income;

  public static float CalcMonthlyIncome(float hourlyWages) {
    Console.WriteLine(" Monthly income is "+hourlyWages * 160);
    return hourlyWages * 160;
  }

  public static float CalcAnnualIncome(float hourlyWages) {
    Console.WriteLine(" Annual income is "+hourlyWages * 12*
                                                          160);
    return hourlyWages * 160 * 12;
  }
}
```

 |

In [Listing 18.4](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec2.html_ch18list04) the `AllIncomes` delegate is obtained by adding `MonthlyIncome` and `AnnualIncome`. As a result, when the `AllIncomes` delegate is invoked, both `MonthlyIncome` and `AnnualIncome` get called. If any of the methods throws an `exception`, then the subsequent methods do not get called. You can use the invocation list of the delegate to gain finer control of the list of functions that can be called, as shown in [Listing 18.5](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec2.html_ch18list05).

##### Listing 18.5\. Using the `GetInvocationList` (C#)

|  
```
 using System;

public class Test {

  public delegate float CalcIncome(float hourlyWages);

  public static readonly CalcIncome MonthlyIncome = new
                     CalcIncome(Person.CalcMonthlyIncome);

  public static readonly CalcIncome AnnualIncome = new
                       CalcIncome(Person.CalcAnnualIncome);

  public static readonly CalcIncome AllIncomes = MonthlyIncome
                                                 + AnnualIncome;

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    try {
        foreach (CalcIncome del in
          AllIncomes.GetInvocationList())
        {
          del(40);
        }
      } catch(Exception e) {
      Console.WriteLine(e.StackTrace);
    }
  }
}

public class Person {

  public float income;
  public static float CalcMonthlyIncome(float hourlyWages) {
    Console.WriteLine(" Monthly income is " +hourlyWages *
                                                          160);
    return hourlyWages * 160;
  }
  public static float CalcAnnualIncome(float hourlyWages) {
    Console.WriteLine(" Annual income is "+hourlyWages * 12*
                                                          160);
    return hourlyWages * 160 * 12;
  }
}
```

 |

The next section looks at how delegates can be used to do event-based programming in C#.

### 18.3\. Event Programming

If you have done Win32 GUI-based or Java Swing/AWT-based programming, you are probably familiar with event programming. If you have dabbled in JavaBeans, you are probably familiar with the concept of listeners listening to changes to a JavaBeans property, and you know how these listeners can be added or deleted dynamically. Listeners in Java are essentially classes whose methods get called when a particular event happens. An event is also a class that is generated by yet another class, called the source. Because everything in Java is modeled as a class, it is sometimes confusing to differentiate a listener (the event receiver) from the source (the event generator).

Whether in Java or C#, an event is a message sent by an object to signal the occurrence of an action. The action can be triggered by a GUI control or by a daemon process. Every event has an event sender and one or more event receivers. The senders and receivers are totally unaware of each other.

In C#, delegates are used to tie the sender and the receiver. As explained earlier in this chapter, a delegate is a type-safe function pointer. When a source generates an event, an event object is instantiated and filled with properties called event arguments. The event object is then passed to a delegate, which gets invoked. An event listener registers or deregisters its interest in the event by adding or removing its own delegate to the event handler delegate. The .NET Framework provides an `event` keyword. An event, then, is essentially a delegate with a very specific signature. Events are usually declared `public`, although other access modifiers can be used.

To illustrate the basics of event programming, we will introduce the various components. [Listing 18.6](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec3.html_ch18list06) shows an event source class. All events originate from a source.

##### Listing 18.6\. The Event Source (C#)

|  
```
 using System;

public delegate void TornadoHandler(object sender, EventArgs
                                                             e);

public delegate void HurricaneHandler(object sender, EventArgs
                                                             e);

//The source of all events
abstract public class Weather {
  abstract protected void OnEvent(EventArgs args);
  public void Happen() {
    OnEvent(EventArgs.Empty);
  }
}
public class Tornado : Weather {
  public event TornadoHandler myEvent ;
  protected override void OnEvent(EventArgs args) {
    if (myEvent != null) {
        myEvent (this, args);
    }
  }
}
public class Hurricane : Weather {
  public event HurricaneHandler myEvent ;
  protected override void OnEvent(EventArgs args) {
    if (myEvent != null) {
        myEvent(this, args);
    }
  }
}
```

 |

In this case the `Weather` class is the source of the event. It is an `abstract` class and has two subclasses (`Tornado` and `Hurricane`), each specifying its respective events. The `Happen()` method calls the `OnEvent()` method with an empty `EventArgs` argument. Because we are overriding the method in the subclass, the `OnEvent` method of the subclass gets called, and the respective `event` is generated. In this case there is no `event` object as such; instead, the communication is done through the `EventArgs` argument.

The listener of the events is shown in [Listing 18.7](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec3.html_ch18list07), which is the `BasicWeatherStation` class.

##### Listing 18.7\. The Event Listener (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
public class BasicWeatherStation {

  public BasicWeatherStation () {
  }
  public void AddWeather2Watch(Weather weather) {
    Tornado tor = weather as Tornado;
    if (tor != null) {
      tor.myEvent += new
           TornadoHandler(BasicTornadoHandler);
    }
    Hurricane cane = weather as Hurricane;
    if (cane != null) {
      cane.myEvent += new
             HurricaneHandler(BasicHurricaneHandler);
    }
  }

  public void BasicTornadoHandler(object sender, EventArgs e) {
    Console.WriteLine("Station has issued a tornado watch");
}
  public void BasicHurricaneHandler(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Station has issued a hurricane warning");
  }

  public static void Main(string[] args) {

    Weather tornado = new Tornado();
    Weather hurricane = new Hurricane();
    BasicWeatherStation station = new
                 BasicWeatherStation();
    station.AddWeather2Watch(tornado);
    station.AddWeather2Watch(hurricane);
    tornado.Happen();
    hurricane.Happen();
  }
}
```

 |

The weather station class is interested in knowing about all sorts of weather and therefore has weather event handlers for each type of weather. The `BasicWeatherStation` class registers its interest in knowing about the weather by adding its event handlers `BasicTornadoHandler` and `BasicHurricaneHandler` to the respective event delegates of the specific weathers, as shown in [Listing 18.8](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec3.html_ch18list08).

##### Listing 18.8\. Adding Event Handlers to Event Delegates (C#)

|  
```
 Tornado tor = weather as Tornado;
if (tor != null) {
  tor.myEvent += new
  TornadoHandler(BasicTornadoHandler);
}
Hurricane cane = weather as Hurricane;
if (cane != null) {
  cane.myEvent += new
  HurricaneHandler(BasicHurricaneHandler);
}
```

 |

The output of [Listing 18.8](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec3.html_ch18list08) is as follows:

```
 Station has issued a tornado watch
Station has issued a hurricane warning
```

In this example the subclasses take care of declaring the specific events and must implement the code in the `OnEvent` method even though the code is similar for both subclasses.

It is possible for the `weather` class to maintain an internal map of delegates that will get called based on a specific key. [Listing 18.9](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec3.html_ch18list09) shows a smarter `Weather` class, which is no longer `abstract`. The `Weather` class now implements an internal map of weather types to actual handlers. All tornadoes are handled by `BasicWeatherStation.BasicTornadoHandler`, and all hurricanes are handled by `BasicWeatherStation.BasicHurricaneHandler`.

##### Listing 18.9\. The New `Weather` Class (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Collections;

public delegate void WeatherHandler(object sender, EventArgs e);
public class Weather {

  string key;
  static Hashtable weathers = new Hashtable();
  public Weather (string key, WeatherHandler wh) {
    this.key = key;
    weathers[key] = (WeatherHandler)weathers[key] + wh;
  }
  public event WeatherHandler weatherEvent
  {
    add
    {
      weathers[key]
        Delegate.Combine(( Delegate)weathers[key], value);
    }
    remove
    {
      weathers[key] = Delegate.Remove((
        Delegate)weathers[key], value);
    }
  }

  public void Happen() {
    OnEvent(EventArgs.Empty);
  }
  protected void OnEvent(EventArgs args) {
    WeatherHandler wh = (WeatherHandler) weathers[key];
    wh(this, args);
  }
}
```

 |

Note that the compiler provides default implementation of the `add` and `remove` methods of the `event` keyword. In the class in [Listing 18.9](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec3.html_ch18list09) we chose to implement our own versions of these methods so that the delegate instances are stored in a central hash table. This class also uses the `static` methods of the `Delegate` class as opposed to using the “+” and “-” operators. The `Weather` constructor now registers the passed-in `WeatherHandler` with the internal map. The `Happen()` method calls the `OnEvent` method, which, based on the `key` field of the `Weather` class, picks up the appropriate event delegate and invokes it.

[Listing 18.10](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec3.html_ch18list10) shows the corresponding `BasicWeatherStation` class. The usage of the delegates is simplified. Most of the work is done by the `Weather` class. The `BasicWeatherStation` is used only for the callback methods.

##### Listing 18.10\. The New `BasicWeatherStation` Class (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
public class BasicWeatherStation {

  public static void BasicTornadoHandler(object sender,
                                               EventArgs e) {
    Console.WriteLine("Station has issued a tornado watch");
  }
  public static void BasicHurricaneHandler(object sender,
                                           EventArgs e) {
    Console.WriteLine("Station has issued a hurricane
                                                     warning");
  }

  public static void Main(string[] args) {

    Weather tornado = new Weather ("Tornado", new
      WeatherHandler(BasicWeatherStation.BasicTornadoHandler));

    Weather hurricane = new Weather("Hurricane", new
    Weather(BasicWeatherStation.BasicHurricaneHandler));

    tornado.Happen();
    hurricane.Happen();
  }
}
```

 |

So far we have registered the weather listeners based on the type of the weather—tornado or hurricane. This may not seem specific enough because multiple listeners could be interested in a particular tornado, and a listener could be interested in knowing about multiple tornadoes. Also, there is no way to inform all stations of a particular event. [Listing 18.11](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec3.html_ch18list11) shows a modified version of the `Weather` class.

##### Listing 18.11\. Modified Version of the `Weather` Class (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Collections;

public delegate void WeatherHandler(object sender,
                                       EventArgs e);

public class Weather {

  string key;
  object station;
  static Hashtable weathers = new Hashtable();
  private Weather(){}

  public static void AddHandlers(string key, IStation station) {
    Hashtable stationHandlers = (Hashtable) weathers[station];
    if (stationHandlers == null) {
      stationHandlers = new Hashtable();
      stationHandlers[key] = station.GetHandler(key);
      weathers[station] = stationHandlers;
    } else {

      stationHandlers[key] = (WeatherHandler)
      stationHandlers[key] + station.GetHandler(key);
    }
  }

  public static void Happen(string key, IStation station) {

    Hashtable stationHandlers = (Hashtable) weathers[station];
    if (stationHandlers == null) {
      stationHandlers = new Hashtable();
      stationHandlers[key] = station.GetHandler(key);
      weathers[station] = stationHandlers;
    }
    WeatherHandler wh = (WeatherHandler) stationHandlers[key];
    wh(new Weather(), EventArgs.Empty);
  }

  public static void Happen(string key) {
    ICollection keys = weathers.Keys;
    foreach (object o in keys) {
      Hashtable handlers = (Hashtable) weathers[o];
      WeatherHandler wh = (WeatherHandler) handlers[key];
      wh(new Weather(), EventArgs.Empty);
    }
    if (keys.Count == 0)
      throw new ArgumentException("No station is interested in
                                                   {0} ", key);
  }

}
```

 |

To maintain the many-to-many relationship between the weather type and the weather station, the `Weather` class maintains a `static Hashtable` of `Hashtable`s. The primary `Hashtable` is keyed off the `station` object. The secondary (or inner) `Hashtable` is keyed off the weather type, where the value is the handler delegate. This data structure allows us to query for the following:

*   All handlers of a given weather type regardless of the station

*   The handler of a specific station and a specific weather

*   All handlers of a specific station and a specific weather

Handlers of a particular station and weather type are registered using the `AddHandlers` method. This method takes care of storing the delegates to be called based on the station and the `weather` type. The `Happen` method is overloaded. The two-argument version notifies a specific station of a specific event. The single-argument version notifies all handlers of all stations for a given weather.

[Listing 18.12](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec3.html_ch18list12) implements the listener classes. The two weather stations implement an `IStation` interface and indicate which delegate is to be used for which weather type. In the `Main` method we then register the stations (listeners) with the `Weather`. Depending on the `Happen` method called, the weather stations are notified.

##### Listing 18.12\. Entry Point and Driver for [Listing 18.11](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec3.html_ch18list11) (C#)

|  
```
 using System;

public class BasicWeatherStation : IStation {

  public void BasicTornadoHandler(object sender, EventArgs e) {
    Console.WriteLine("Station has issued a tornado watch");
  }

  public void BasicHurricaneHandler(object sender, EventArgs e) {
    Console.WriteLine("Station has issued a hurricane warning");
  }

  public WeatherHandler GetHandler(string key) {
    if ("Tornado".Equals(key)) {
      return new WeatherHandler(BasicTornadoHandler);
    } else if ("Hurricane".Equals(key)) {
      return new WeatherHandler(BasicHurricaneHandler);
    }
    throw new ArgumentException("Can handle only
                  Tornadoes and Hurricanes at this time");
  }

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    BasicWeatherStation station1 = new BasicWeatherStation();
    AdvancedWeatherStation station2 = new AdvancedWeather
                                                   Station();

    Weather.AddHandlers("Tornado", station1);
    Weather.AddHandlers("Tornado", station2);
    Weather.AddHandlers("Hurricane", station1);
    Weather.AddHandlers("Hurricane", station2);

    //Response of all stations interested in the tornado
    Weather.Happen("Tornado");

    //Station2's response to the hurricane
    Weather.Happen("Hurricane", station2);
  }
}

public class AdvancedWeatherStation : IStation {

  public void AdvancedTornadoHandler(object sender,
                                       EventArgs e) {
    Console.WriteLine("Advanced Station
                   has issued a tornado watch");
  }

  public void AdvancedHurricaneHandler(object sender, EventArgs
                                                           e) {
    Console.WriteLine("Advanced Station
                  has issued a hurricane warning");
  }

  public WeatherHandler GetHandler(string key) {

    if ("Tornado".Equals(key)) {
      return new WeatherHandler(AdvancedTornadoHandler);
    } else if ("Hurricane".Equals(key)) {
      return new WeatherHandler(AdvancedHurricaneHandler);
    }
    throw new ArgumentException("Can handle only
                  Tornadoes and Hurricanes at this time");
  }
}
public interface IStation {
  WeatherHandler GetHandler(string key);
}
```

 |

The output of the forecast in [Listing 18.12](#0672324024_ch18lev1sec3.html_ch18list12) is as follows:

```
 Advanced Station has issued a tornado watch
Station has issued a tornado watch
Advanced Station has issued a hurricane warning
```

From the prior discussions it should be clear that the event programming paradigm in C# is similar to JavaBeans programming. Essentially, listeners interested in the property change register themselves with the property. When the property is changed, each of the registered listeners is notified of the change. In Java, the event receiver (listener), event generator (source), and the event itself are all classes. In C#, the event itself is modeled as a delegate callback.

### 18.4\. Summary

C# delegates can be thought of as type-safe function pointers. Function pointers are essentially references to actual functions. A delegate can also wrap a call to a series of functions that can be added or deleted dynamically. Because of the indirect nature of the function call, delegates are useful for simulating asynchronous method calls (such as calls to the `System.Threading` and `System.IO` namespaces). Delegates are also used in event-based programming in C#. Event programming in C# is similar to the JavaBeans property change listener paradigm. Because you can add or delete functions to a delegate, which in turn points to multiple functions, delegates can conveniently simulate the JavaBeans property change listener paradigm.

## Chapter 19\. Accessing Databases

An enterprise application usually has a relational database management system (RBDMS) as its backend data storage. Most enterprise applications involve a component that interacts with these RDBMS systems. Not surprisingly, both Java and C# come equipped with APIs that make it a breeze to access and work with databases. C# uses the ADO.NET API, which is not limited to accessing relational databases. In fact the API is not limited to accessing databases at all. In theory, you can use ADO.NET to access any kind of data store, including object-oriented database management systems (OODBMSs), data files, and e-mail messages. Java's JDBC 3.0 API is focused on accessing RDBMSs.

This chapter discusses the C# APIs only in the context of accessing an RDBMS. It is assumed that you are familiar with the concept of an RDBMS and with Structured Query Language (SQL) syntax.

### 19.1\. Inside ADO.NET

ActiveX Data Objects (ADO) was designed to be a high-level interface to provide ease of access to a wide variety of data sources. ADO.NET was evolved from ADO and has become Microsoft's standard API of access to data sources. Traditional database access is a two-tier approach in which a live connection to the database is maintained. This approach does not scale well for multitier applications in which data must be transferred from one tier to another. By using an XML representation of the data obtained from the database or an XML stream, ADO.NET provides disconnected access to data, thereby scaling better in n-tier applications.

ADO.NET abstracts the concept of data storage into a data source. Examples of data sources are an RDBMS, an OODBMS, data files, and e-mail messages.

The C# API for accessing databases is packaged in four namespaces (see [Table 19.1](#0672324024_ch19lev1sec1.html_ch19table01)).

The two key concepts of ADO.NET are the .NET data provider and the `DataSet` object as shown in [Figure 19.1](#0672324024_ch19lev1sec1.html_ch19fig01). We look first at the .NET data provider, which is a set of classes for interfacing with a data source. A .NET data provider consists of all classes necessary to connect to the data source, issue commands to the data source, and retrieve and update the data from the data source. Similarly, the classes of a typical .NET data provider can be categorized as follows:

*   `Connection`. Class for connecting to the database

*   `Command`. An abstraction for specifying random SQL commands, with parameters to the underlying RDBMS source

*   `DataReader`. A lightweight class for read-only forward movement on the set of results obtained by running a query

*   `DataAdapter`. A set of classes used for selecting data or doing updates, inserts, and deletes to the data source

##### Figure 19.1\. The ADO.NET Object Model

![](0672324024_ch19lev1sec1_image01.gif)

Table 19.1\. C# Namespaces for Accessing Databases

| Namespace | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `System.Data` | This namespace consists of most of the core classes for accessing the database. |
| `System.Data.SqlTypes` | This namespace provides classes for native data types within SQL Server. These classes provide a safe, fast alternative to other data types. Using the classes in this namespace helps prevent type conversion errors in situations where loss of precision could occur. Because other data types are converted to and from `SqlType`s behind the scenes, explicitly creating and using objects within this namespace also results in faster code. |
| `System.Data.Commons` | This namespace contains classes shared by the .NET data providers. |
| `System.Data.OleDb` | This namespace contains all the classes for the OLE DB provider. |
| `System.Data.SqlClient` | This namespace contains all the classes for the SQL Server provider. |

There are two .NET data providers. The SQL Server data provider consists of classes that are optimized specifically for accessing the Microsoft SQL Server database. These classes are in the `System.Data.SqlClient` namespace. The OLE DB data provider consists of classes for accessing any other database (Oracle, Sybase, and so on). Classes for this data provider can be found in the `System.Data.OleDb` namespace.

The other concept of ADO.NET is the `DataSet` object. A `DataSet` object is an in-memory cache of data retrieved from the database. The `DataSet` object tries to mimic the tabular structure of the underlying database. The `DataSet` object consists of a collection of objects that mimic RDBMS concepts such as tables, table relations, columns, rows, and constraints. A `DataSet` reads and writes data and schemata as XML documents. The data and schemata can be transported via HTTP and used by any application on any platform that is XML-enabled.

### 19.2\. JDBC 2.0+

The Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) API contains two major sets of interfaces: the JDBC API for application writers, and the lower-level JDBC driver API for driver writers.

The central piece of database access in Java is the database driver, the software that translates the JDBC calls from the application into native calls that the database can understand. The JDBC driver is the equivalent of the .NET data provider, but unlike the .NET data provider, the JDBC driver is more of a black box that sits between the database and the application. Most application developers do not need to know the guts of the driver because they interact with it only through the JDBC API. Various RDBMS vendors (Oracle, IBM, Sybase, and so on) supply JDBC-compliant drivers for their individual databases.

An application typically uses one of four types of database drivers:

*   Type 1: JDBC-ODBC bridge plus ODBC driver. This combination provides JDBC access via ODBC drivers.

*   Type 2: A native-API, partly Java-technology-enabled driver. This type of driver converts JDBC calls into calls on the client API for Oracle, Sybase, Informix, DB2, or other DBMSs. This style of driver requires that some binary code be loaded on each client machine.

*   Type 3: Pure Java driver for database middleware. This style of driver translates JDBC calls into the middleware vendor's protocol, which is then translated to a DBMS protocol by a middleware server.

*   Type 4: Direct-to-database pure Java driver. This style of driver converts JDBC calls into the network protocol used directly by DBMSs, allowing a direct call from the client machine to the DBMS server and providing a practical solution for intranet access.

Modern-day drivers tend to be of type 4\. The JDBC API provides everything you need to access a database. The API is not geared to favor any one particular database, and therefore you can use the same JDBC code for different databases.

ADO.NET supports an API for accessing most data sources; however, it also supplies a set of separate, performance-optimized classes for accessing the Microsoft SQL Server database. If your application is pretty much tied to Microsoft SQL Server and if code portability is not a concern for you, then you can leverage this vendor-centric API to boost application performance.

### 19.3\. Getting Started with ADO.NET

Before you can understand the features of the C# API, you need to have a database server and a sample database to access. The focus of this chapter is to demonstrate the API and not the tools, so we do not describe the details of setting up a database, database schema, and tables. Instead, we use the standard Northwind database that ships with all Microsoft RDBMSs. We use Microsoft SQL Server as our database. To make the examples work, you need an instance of Microsoft SQL Server running locally on your machine.

We first explore how to accomplish these routine database tasks:

*   Establishing a connection to the database

*   Running a `SELECT` query and getting data

*   Running an `INSERT`, `UPDATE` , or `DELETE` query

*   Running a stored procedure

*   Processing transactions

*   Exploring database metadata

#### 19.3.1\. Establishing a Connection to the Database

[Listing 19.1](#0672324024_ch19lev1sec3.html_ch19list01) shows how to open a connection to the database using the `SqlClient` provider and the `OleDb` provider. You use different connection classes depending on the provider you want to use for connecting. Fortunately, `IDbConnection` is a common interface implemented by these two classes, so we can use that interface to do the two most important connection-related tasks, which are basically opening and closing the connection.

Note that we specify the connection properties using the `ConnectionString` property of the connection object. The `ConnectionString` uses the following format:

```
 "key1=valuel;key2=value2";
```

Keys are not case-sensitive. If a key name occurs more than once in the connection string, the value associated with the last occurrence is used. Note that the `ConnectionString` property is read/write for a closed connection, and read-only for an open connection.

##### Listing 19.1. Establishing a Connection to the Database with ADO.NET (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Data;
using System.Data.OleDb;
using System.Data.SqlClient;

class Test {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {

    IDbConnection conn = null;
    try {
      conn = new OleDbConnection();
      conn.ConnectionString = "Provider=SQLOLEDB;Initial
        Catalog=Northwind;Data Source=localhost;Integrated
                                           Security=SSPI;";
      conn.Open();
      Console.WriteLine("Connection "+conn);
      conn = new SqlConnection();
      conn.ConnectionString = "Initial Catalog=Northwind;Data
                 Source=localhost;Integrated Security=SSPI;";
      conn.Open();
      Console.WriteLine("Connection "+conn);
    } catch(Exception e) {
      Console.WriteLine(e.StackTrace);
    } finally {
      conn.Close();
    }
  }
}
```

 |

The output of [Listing 19.1](#0672324024_ch19lev1sec3.html_ch19list01) is as follows:

```
 Connection System.Data.OleDb.OleDbConnection
Connection System.Data.SqlClient.SqlConnection
```

Note that the `IDbConnection` interface is conceptually equivalent to `java.sql.Connection`. In Java you must load the driver class and specify the database URL, user, and password to connect to the database:

```
 Class.forName(driverClass).newInstance();
Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user,
password);
```

Unlike Java, which does not have built-in support for connection pooling, ADO.NET provides automatic connection pooling.

#### 19.3.2\. Running a `SELECT` Query and Getting Data

[Listing 19.2](#0672324024_ch19lev1sec3.html_ch19list02) shows a sample of how to use the `OleDb` provider and the `SqlClient` provider to read rows of data returned from a `SELECT` query.

##### Listing 19.2\. Running a `SELECT` Query to Get Data (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Data;
using System.Data.OleDb;
using System.Data.SqlClient;

class Test {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    GetDataUsingOleDb();
    Console.WriteLine("————");
    GetDataUsingSqlClient();
  }
  private static void GetDataUsingOleDb() {
    OleDbConnection conn = null;
    OleDbDataReader reader = null;
    try {
      conn = GetOledbConnection();
      OleDbCommand command = conn.CreateCommand();
      command.CommandText = "SELECT * FROM CUSTOMERS WHERE
                                  UPPER(COUNTRY) = 'GERMANY'";
      reader = command.ExecuteReader();
      Console.Write("Customer ID \t\t Contact Name \n");
      while (reader.Read()) {
        Console.Write(reader.GetString(1));
        Console.Write("\t\t\t");
        Console.WriteLine(reader.GetString(3));
      }
    } finally {
      if (reader != null) reader.Close();
      if (conn != null) conn.Close();
    }
  }
  private static void GetDataUsingSqlClient() {
    SqlConnection conn = null;
    SqlDataReader reader = null;
    try {
      conn = GetSQLConnection();
      SqlCommand command = conn.CreateCommand();
      command.CommandText = "SELECT * FROM CUSTOMERS WHERE
                                  UPPER(COUNTRY) = 'GERMANY'";
      reader = command.ExecuteReader();
      Console.Write("Customer ID \t\t Company Name \n");
      while (reader.Read()) {
        Console.Write(reader.GetString(1));
        Console.Write("\t\t\t");
        Console.WriteLine(reader.GetString(2));
      }
    } finally {
       if (reader != null) reader.Close();
       if (conn != null) conn.Close();
    }
  }

  private static OleDbConnection GetOledbConnection() {
    OleDbConnection conn = new OleDbConnection();
    conn.ConnectionString = "provider=SQLOLEDB;Initial
      Catalog=Northwind;Data Source=localhost;Integrated
                                               Security=SSPI;";
    conn.Open();
    return conn;
  }
  private static SqlConnection GetSQLConnection() {
    SqlConnection conn = new SqlConnection();
    conn.ConnectionString = "Initial Catalog=Northwind;Data
                   Source=localhost;Integrated Security=SSPI;";
    conn.Open();
    return conn;
  }

}
```

 |

Ottilies Käseladen                Henriette Pfalzheim
QUICK-Stop                        Horst Kloss
Toms Spezialitäten                Karin Josephs
Die Wandernde Kuh                 Rita Muller
```

The basic idea is to create a `SqlCommand` or an `OleDbCommand` that is conceptually equivalent to the `java.sql.PreparedStatement` class of Java. The command then executes the query using the `ExecuteQuery` method. The method returns a `SqlDataReader` or an `OleDbDataReader`, respectively. This is conceptually equivalent to the action of the `java.sql.ResultSet` class.

One similarity that might help Java developers is that the readers do not provide methods to retrieve the column data given the column name. This implies that you don't have to be familiar with the order of the columns that are being returned by the query. Note that the first column is obtained using the order 0 and not 1 (as in Java). The `java.sql.ResultSet` allows access by either column order or column name.

[Listing 19.3](#0672324024_ch19lev1sec3.html_ch19list03) shows how to use the `ExecuteScalar` method of the command. This method is a convenience method that is useful when you know that you are fetching only one-column data from the query. Java does not provide such a convenience method, and therefore you must use code something like this:

```
 ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery();
If (rs.next()) {
  int count = rs.getInt(1);
}
```

[Listing 19.3](#0672324024_ch19lev1sec3.html_ch19list03) also shows how you can use interfaces instead of concrete classes to write provider-agnostic code.

##### Listing 19.3\. Using the `ExecuteScalar` Function (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Data;
using System.Data.OleDb;
using System.Data.SqlClient;

class Test {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    GetData();
  }
  private static void GetData() {
    IDbConnection conn = null;
    try {
      conn = GetConnection();
      IDbCommand command = conn.CreateCommand();
      command.CommandText = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMERS
                            WHERE UPPER(COUNTRY) = 'GERMANY'";
      Console.WriteLine("Number of customers from Germany =
                                    "+command.ExecuteScalar());
    } finally {
      if (conn != null) conn.Close();
    }
  }

  private static IDbConnection GetConnection()

    SqlConnection conn = new SqlConnection();
    conn.ConnectionString = "Initial Catalog=Northwind;Data
                   Source=localhost;Integrated Security=SSPI;";
    conn.Open();
    return conn;
  }

}
```

 |

The output of [Listing 19.3](#0672324024_ch19lev1sec3.html_ch19list03) is as follows:

 Number of customers from Germany = 11
```

So far we have seen `SELECT` queries in which the query is complete in itself, meaning that no parameters are bound at runtime. [Listing 19.4](#0672324024_ch19lev1sec3.html_ch19list04) shows how to bind parameters at runtime.

##### Listing 19.4\. Binding Parameters at Runtime (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Data;
using System.Data.OleDb;
using System.Data.SqlClient;

class Test {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    GetData();
  }
  private static void GetData() {
    IDbConnection conn = null;
    try {
      conn = GetConnection();
      IDbCommand command = conn.CreateCommand();
      command.CommandText = "SELECT * FROM CUSTOMERS
                                       WHERE UPPER(Country)=?";
      command.Parameters.Add(new
                 OleDbParameter("Country", "USA"));
      IDataReader reader = command.ExecuteReader();
      while (reader.Read()) {
        Console.WriteLine(reader.GetString(1));
      }
    } finally {
      if (conn != null) conn.Close();
    }
  }

  private static IDbConnection GetConnection() {
    OleDbConnection conn = new OleDbConnection();
    conn.ConnectionString = "Provider=SQLOLEDB;Initial
      Catalog=Northwind;Data Source=localhost;Integrated
                                               Security=SSPI;";
    conn.Open();
    return conn;
  }

}
```

You bind the parameters by instantiating either an `OleDbParameter` or a `SQLParameter` and then simply adding it to the collection of the command object. The order in which the parameters are added is the same order in which they appear in the query.

#### 19.3.3\. Running an `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` Query

[Listing 19.5](#0672324024_ch19lev1sec3.html_ch19list05) shows an example that runs an `INSERT`, an `UPDATE`, and a `DELETE` query.

##### Listing 19.5\. Doing Insert, Update, and Delete (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Data;
using System.Data.OleDb;
using System.Data.SqlClient;

class Test {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    InsertData();
    UpdateData();
    DeleteData();
  }
  private static void InsertData() {
    IDbConnection conn = null;
    try {
      conn = GetConnection();
      IDbCommand command = conn.CreateCommand();
      command.CommandText = "INSERT INTO CUSTOMERS (CUSTOMERID,
                     COMPANYNAME, CONTACTNAME) VALUES (?,?,?)";
      command.Prepare();
      command.Parameters.Add(new OleDbParameter("CustomerID",
                                                     "ACME3"));
      command.Parameters.Add(new OleDbParameter("CompanyName",
                                           "Acme Object Inc"));
      command.Parameters.Add(new OleDbParameter("ContactName",
                                                "Mr. Object"));
      command.ExecuteNonQuery();
    } finally {
       if (conn != null) conn.Close();
    }
  }
  private static void UpdateData() {
    IDbConnection conn = null;
    try {
      conn = GetConnection();
      IDbCommand command = conn.CreateCommand();
      command.CommandText = "UPDATE CUSTOMERS SET
                  COMPANYNAME = ? WHERE CUSTOMERID = ?";
      command.Prepare();
      command.Parameters.Add(new OleDbParameter("CompanyName",
                                              "Acme Object "));
      command.Parameters.Add(new OleDbParameter("CustomerID",
                                                     "ACME3"));
      command.ExecuteNonQuery();
    } finally {
       if (conn != null) conn.Close();
    }
  }
  private static void DeleteData() {
    IDbConnection conn = null;
    try {
      conn = GetConnection();
      IDbCommand command = conn.CreateCommand();
      command.CommandText = "DELETE FROM CUSTOMERS
                                         WHERE CUSTOMERID = ?";
      command.Prepare();
      command.Parameters.Add(new
        OleDbParameter("CustomerID", "ACME3"));
      command.ExecuteNonQuery();
    } finally {
       if (conn != null) conn.Close();
    }
  }

  private static IDbConnection GetConnection() {
    OleDbConnection conn = new OleDbConnection();
    conn.ConnectionString = "Provider=SQLOLEDB;Initial
                  Catalog=Northwind;Data Source=localhost;
                                     Integrated Security=SSPI;";
    conn.Open();
    return conn;
  }

}
```

 |

The output of [Listing 19.5](#0672324024_ch19lev1sec3.html_ch19list05) must be verified by querying the database. It effectively inserts a row, updates it, and then deletes it. The following line returns an `int` indicating the number of rows that were affected by the insert, update, or delete query.

```
 command.ExecuteNonQuery();
```

Note that the use of the `Prepare()` method on the `IDbCommand` compiles the statement for future execution. This may not be a concern in this program, but in an application that executes a SQL query several times, you can improve perfor mance by running the compiled version of the `command` object.
