![](0672324024_ch21lev1sec2_image06.gif)

Using the IDE GUI toolkit is fairly intuitive. Here is the overall procedure for quickly creating controls and coding them:

| **1.** | Double-click or drag any of the controls onto the form. 
 |
| **2.** | Right-click on the control and change any properties you want. The Properties box also shows the events that can be associated with that control. You specify the name of the method that gets called when the event is fired on that control. 
 |
| **3.** | Add code to the relevant event methods associated with the control. 
 |

Unlike the AWT and Swing libraries—which have layout managers that take care of resizing the contained controls when the container is resized—the Windows library does not have layout managers. The position of the controls is specified in absolute terms with respect to the container. This is similar to the absolute position layout of Java. As a result, when you resize a form window, the controls inside that form window do not resize along with the form. In [Section 21.5](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec5.html_ch21lev1sec5) you will learn about docking and anchoring controls with respect to the container, thereby allowing the controls to resize along with the form.

Now that you've seen how easy it is to create a simple application using the IDE GUI toolkit, you are encouraged to play with the Form Designer as much as possible and discover the different pathways for editing code and designing screens.

### 21.3\. Windows Forms, Component Controls, and Their Associated .NET Classes

As shown in [Table 21.1](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec3.html_ch21table01), four namespaces contain all the GUI-related classes.

For our purposes, this chapter explores only those classes in the `System.Windows.Form`s namespace. Classes in this namespace can be categorized as controls, components, and common dialog boxes. Controls are GUI widgets that display information to the user. They handle user input through the keyboard and pointing devices. They also handle message routing and security. Controls have associated properties and events and are represented by classes that inherit from the `System.Windows.Form.Control` class.

[Table 21.2](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec3.html_ch21table02) shows a subset of the controls in the Visual Studio .NET default toolbox, along with their associated .NET classes. The Java Swing equivalents of these classes are given for easy reference.

The component classes are helper classes that are used to model GUI components typical of a Windows application. Component classes typically inherit from the `System.ComponentModel.Component` class. [Table 21.3](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec3.html_ch21table03) shows the components and their associated .NET classes.

Table 21.1\. .NET GUI Namespaces

| Namespace | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `System.Windows.Forms` | Classes in this namespace can be categorized as controls, components, and dialog boxes. Controls are GUI widgets (such as textboxes and check-boxes); MDI or SDI forms; or custom user controls. Components are classes used in conjunction with controls to build rich Windows applications (such as ToolTips, Windows help, and the menu framework). Common dialog boxes model the commonly encountered Windows pop-up dialog boxes that are displayed when users do tasks such as open or save a file, select a font, or print. |
| `System.Windows.Forms.ComponentModel`, `System.Windows.Forms.Design, System.Windows.Forms.PropertyGridInternal` | These namespaces contain classes that can be used to extend design-time support for Windows Forms. |
| `System.Drawing` | Classes in this namespace provide access to GDI+ basic graphics functionality. |

Common dialog boxes represent those components that are common to the Windows operating system and that can be leveraged in a C# application. The classes of these components inherit from the `System.Windows.Forms.CommonDialog` class. [Table 21.4](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec3.html_ch21table04) shows the dialog boxes and their .NET classes.

Associated with every control, component, and dialog box class are properties and events. Properties can be set at design time or dynamically. You specify events by indicating the delegate that will be used upon the execution of the event. For example, a form control has an associated `Load` event. This event is fired whenever the form is loaded, much like the `onload` event of the HTML body tag. Using the .NET IDE or dynamically, you can specify the delegate that is associated with this `Load` event. You specify the event delegate as follows:

```
 this.Load += new System.EventHandler(this.
  PersonDetailForm_Load);
```

### 21.4\. Putting It All Together

In this section we will demonstrate a simple GUI front end. We will use the .NET IDE to assemble the GUI controls, sparing ourselves the tedium of specifying their design-time display properties. We will then add code to the relevant pieces to make these controls interactive. [Figure 21.7](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec4.html_ch21fig07) shows a snapshot of the application.

##### Figure 21.7\. The People Browser

![](0672324024_ch21lev1sec4_image01.gif)

#### 21.4.1\. What the Application Does

The application allows the user to open and load an XML file (of a specific format) that contains data about `Person` objects. It then displays the parsed data in GUI controls for easy browsing.

#### 21.4.2\. Source Files of the Application

To see a list of the source files making up your application, click on View and then click on Solutions Explorer in the .NET IDE. For simplicity we have adopted the Java style of specifying only one class per source file and naming the source file the same as the class file. The classes that make up the application are listed in [Table 21.5](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec4.html_ch21table05).

Table 21.5\. Classes in the Sample GUI Application

| Source File | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `Person.cs` | Models the `Person` class. The `Person` object consists of a few properties and a list of addresses and contact info objects. A `Person` object is stored as a `<Person>` tag in the XML file. |
| `Address.cs` | Models the `Address` class. The `Address` object consists of a few properties. An address object is stored as an `<Address>` tag in the XML file. |
| `ContactInfo.cs` | Models a person's phone number or e-mail address. A `Person` object maintains the list of phone numbers and e-mail addresses. Although in the GUI we differentiate between phone and e-mail, the data structure used to store the two is the `ContactInfo` object. |
| `MainForm.cs` | This is the main window of the application. The main form divides the window into the tree of persons (in the left side of the window) and the right side panel, which consists of the `PersonDetailForm`. |
| `PersonDetailForm.cs` | This form shows the details of a `Person` object. The details are further split into two horizontal panels. The upper panel shows the `last-name`, `first-name`, `username`, `password`, and `sex` of the person, and the bottom panel shows a tab control of the addresses, e-mails, and phone information of the person. |
| `PersonNode.cs` | This is a wrapper class for the `Person` class and represents a node of the `Person` tree shown on the main window. By having this class, we avoid adding the `Person` object directly to the tree and thereby prevent having the `Person` class (a non-GUI class) inherit from `TreeNode` (a GUI class). |

Table 21.6\. Controls in the Sample GUI Application

| Control ID | Control |
| --- | --- |
| A | `System.Windows.Forms.Form` |
| B | `System.Windows.Forms.Panel` |
| C | `System.Windows.Forms.TreeView` |
| D | `System.Windows.Forms.ListView` |
| E | `System.Windows.Forms.TextBox` |
| F | `System.Windows.Forms.RadioButton` |
| G | `System.Windows.Forms.TabControl` |
| H | `System.Windows.Forms.MainMenu` |
| I | `System.Windows.Forms.OpenFileDialog` |
| J | `System.Windows.Forms.GroupBox` |

The entire application's GUI components are defined in the `MainForm` and `PersonDetailForm` classes. The rest of the classes manage the interaction between the two form classes. For a clean and maintainable design, it is imperative to separate the GUI classes from the non-GUI classes and to minimize the coupling between the two types of classes. By having first-class objects such as `Person`, `Address`, and `ContactInfo`, you avoid regurgitating that information in every form you design.

#### 21.4.3\. The Application Controls

[Table 21.6](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec4.html_ch21table06) lists the controls used in the application. The properties and the event delegates of the controls are specified at design time.

##### `MainForm.cs`

The contents of `MainForm.cs` are shown in [Listing 21.3](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec4.html_ch21list03).

##### Listing 21.3. `MainForm.cs` (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Drawing;
using System.Collections;
using System.ComponentModel;
using System.Windows.Forms;
using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Data;

namespace Sample {

  public class MainForm : System.Windows.Forms.Form {
    private System.Windows.Forms.Panel DetailPanel;
    private System.Windows.Forms.TreeView tree;
    private System.Windows.Forms.MainMenu mainMenu;
    private System.Windows.Forms.MenuItem menuItem1;
    private System.Windows.Forms.MenuItem menuItem6;
    private System.Windows.Forms.MenuItem openItem;
    private System.Windows.Forms.MenuItem exitItem;
    private System.Windows.Forms.OpenFileDialog openFileDialog;
    private System.Windows.Forms.MenuItem menuItem2;
    private System.Windows.Forms.MenuItem aboutItem;
    private System.ComponentModel.Container components = null;

    public MainForm() {
      InitializeComponent();
    }

    //Entry point
    [STAThread]
    static void Main() {
      Application.Run(new MainForm());
    }

    //Fills up the tree with Person nodes.
    private void FillTree(ArrayList people) {
      tree.BeginUpdate();
      tree.Nodes.Clear();
      foreach (Person p in people) {
        tree.Nodes.Add(new PersonNode(p));
        tree.EndUpdate();
    }

    //Fired when a node is selected on the tree
    private void TreeSelection(object sender,
        System.Windows.Forms.TreeViewEventArgs e) {
      TreeViewAction action = e.Action;
      PersonNode pNode = e.Node as PersonNode;
      //If a person node is clicked
        //show person details on right side
      DetailPanel.Controls.Clear();
      PersonDetailForm f = new PersonDetailForm(pNode.Person);
      DetailPanel.Controls.Add(f.GetMasterPanel());
    }
    //Fired when the user quits the application.
    private void exitItem_Click(object sender,
           System.EventArgs e) {
      Process.GetCurrentProcess().Kill();
    }
    //Fired when user opens a file dialog box for file selection.
    private void file_open(object sender, System.EventArgs e) {
      DialogResult result = openFileDialog.ShowDialog();
      if (result == DialogResult.OK) {
        String file = openFileDialog.FileName;
        ArrayList people = Person.GetPeople(file);
        FillTree(people);
      }
    }

    //Fired when the About menu item is clicked.  
    private void menuItem3_Click(object sender,
           System.EventArgs e) {
      MessageBox.Show(this, "A minimal person browser",
           "People Browser", MessageBoxButtons.OK,
             MessageBoxIcon.Information);
    }
  }
}
```

The `MainForm` class models the main window of the application. [Figure 21.7](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec4.html_ch21fig07) indicates that the main window is split logically into the tree on the left side (defined as the field `tree`) and a detail panel on the right side (defined as `DetailPanel`). The tree consists of `Person` nodes that, when clicked, show details of the `Person` in the detail panel.

[Listing 21.3](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec4.html_ch21list03) does not show the IDE auto-generated code. The entry point of the application is specified by the following lines:

```
 [STAThread]
static void Main() {
  Application.Run(new MainForm());
}
```

After the application starts, the main thread instantiates a `MainForm`. The constructor of the `MainForm` class initializes the form controls. The application is then driven by user actions. If a user clicks on the menu to open a file, the following code is executed:

```
 private void file_open(object sender, System.EventArgs e) {
  DialogResult result = openFileDialog.ShowDialog();
  if (result == DialogResult.OK) {
    String file = openFileDialog.FileName;
    ArrayList people = Person.GetPeople(file);
    FillTree(people);
  }
}
```

This pops up the standard Windows dialog box for opening a file. When the user selects a file, the static method `Person.GetPeople()` parses the XML to create a list of `Person` objects. As the name suggests, the `FillTree()` method fills the tree with `PersonNode` objects.

Note that we add the `PersonNode` objects instead of `Person` objects to the tree. Had we added `Person` objects directly to the tree, they would have to inherit from the `TreeNode` class. Because you can inherit from only one class in C#, by using a `PersonNode` object we keep the view separate from the model `Person` and allow the possibility of the `Person` object inheriting from some other class in the future.

After the tree is filled, you an click on any of the nodes. The following code is invoked when a tree node is selected:

```
 private void TreeSelection(object sender,
       System.Windows.Forms.TreeViewEventArgs e) {
  PersonNode pNode = e.Node as PersonNode;
  DetailPanel.Controls.Clear();
  PersonDetailForm f = new PersonDetailForm(pNode.Person);
  DetailPanel.Controls.Add(f.GetMasterPanel());
}
```

The CLR packages the signal sent by a user clicking on a tree node into the `System.Windows.Forms.TreeViewEventArgs` object. The `Node` attribute of this object indicates the node that was clicked on. When a node is clicked on, we first clear the controls of the right side `DetailPanel`, and then we instantiate a `PersonDetailForm` with the `Person` object clicked on through the node. Because you cannot add a form to a panel, we must add the master panel of the `PersonDetailForm` to the controls of the `DetailPanel`. This takes care of updating the right side of the window with details of the person chosen on the tree.

The contents of `PersonDetailForm.cs` are shown in [Listing 21.4](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec4.html_ch21list04).

```
 using System;

namespace Sample {
  public class PersonDetailForm : System.Windows.Forms.Form {

    private System.ComponentModel.Container components = null;

    private System.Windows.Forms.TabControl Details;

    private System.Windows.Forms.TextBox lastName;
    private System.Windows.Forms.TextBox userName;

    private System.Windows.Forms.Label label2;
    private System.Windows.Forms.Label label3;
    private System.Windows.Forms.Label label4;

    private System.Windows.Forms.RadioButton radioButton2;
    private System.Windows.Forms.TabPage emails;
    private System.Windows.Forms.ListView phoneview;
    private System.Windows.Forms.ListView emailview;
    private System.Windows.Forms.ListView addressview;

    public PersonDetailForm(Person p) {
         InitializeComponent();
      firstName.Text = p.FirstName;
      lastName.Text = p.LastName;
      userName.Text = p.UserName;
      password.Text = p.Password;
      LoadAddressesInView(p);
      LoadContactInfoInView(p, phoneview, p.GetPhones());
      LoadContactInfoInView(p, emailview, p.GetEmails());

    public Control GetMasterPanel() {
        return MasterPanel;

    //Load the phone numbers & e-mails into the view components
    private void LoadContactInfoInView(Person person, ListView
                                                          view,
           ArrayList infos) {
      view.View = View.Details;
      view.Columns.Add("Contact", -2, HorizontalAlignment.
Left);
      view.Columns.Add("Type", -2, HorizontalAlignment.Left);
      view.Columns.Add("Description", -2, HorizontalAlignment.
Left);
      ListViewItem[] items = new ListViewItem[infos.Count];
      for(int i = 0; i < infos.Count; ++i) {
        ContactInfo a = (ContactInfo) infos[i];
        ListViewItem item = new ListViewItem(a.Contact, i);
        item.SubItems.Add(a.Type);
        item.SubItems.Add(a.Description);
          items[i] = item;
      }
      view.Items.AddRange(items);
    }

    //Load the addresses into the view components
    private void LoadAddressesInView(Person person) {
      ArrayList addresses = person.GetAddresses();
      addressview.View = View.Details;
      addressview.Columns.Add("Street", -2,
          HorizontalAlignment.Left);
      addressview.Columns.Add("City", -2,
          HorizontalAlignment.Left);
      addressview.Columns.Add("State", -2,
          HorizontalAlignment.Left);
      addressview.Columns.Add("Zip", -2,
          HorizontalAlignment.Left);
      addressview.Columns.Add("Country", -2,
          HorizontalAlignment.Left);
      ListViewItem[] items = new ListViewItem[addresses.
Count];
      for(int i = 0; i < addresses.Count; ++i) {
        Address a = (Address) addresses[i];
        ListViewItem item = new
            ListViewItem(a.Street.ToString(), i);
        item.SubItems.Add(a.City);
        item.SubItems.Add(a.State);
        item.SubItems.Add(a.Zip);
        item.SubItems.Add(a.Country);
        items[i] = item;
      }
      addressview.Items.AddRange(items);
    }
  }
}
```

The `PersonDetailForm` class models the right side of the main window, which shows the details of the chosen person. The form consists of one panel (the `MasterPanel` field) inside that holds all the components. The main panel contains the top panel (the `TopPanel` field), which in turn contains the person details such as the `lastname`, `firstname`, `sex`, `username`, and `password`. The bottom half of the `MasterPanel` is made up of a tab control (the `Details` field). The tab control consists of three tab pages: `Address`(es) (the `addresses` field), `Phone`(s) (the `phones` field), and `Email`(s) (the `emails` field). Each of the tab pages contains list views (the `addressview` field, `phoneview` field, and `listview` field).

[Listing 21.4](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec4.html_ch21list04) does not show the IDE auto-generated code. The entry point of this form is the form constructor. The constructor takes a `Person` object whose attributes are used to initialize the form GUI controls:

```
 public PersonDetailForm(Person p) {
  InitializeComponent();
  firstName.Text = p.FirstName;
  lastName.Text = p.LastName;
  userName.Text = p.UserName;
  password.Text = p.Password;
  LoadAddressesInView (p);
  LoadContactInfoInView(p, phoneview, p.GetPhones());
  LoadContactInfoInView (p, emailview, p.GetEmails());
}
```

The simple properties of a `Person` object are used to populate the textboxes and radio buttons of the `TopPanel`. The list views at the bottom are filled in the `LoadAddressesInView` and `LoadContactInfoInView` methods. The list views are dynamically defined and filled. The default behavior of the tab controls gives us access to the list views without the need to write any code. The code listings for the non-GUI classes (`Person`, `ContactInfo`, `Address`, and `PersonNode`) are shown in [Listings 21.5](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec4.html_ch21list05), [21.6](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec4.html_ch21list06), [21.7](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec4.html_ch21list07), and [21.8](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec4.html_ch21list08), respectively.

The contents of `Person.cs` are shown in [Listing 21.5](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec4.html_ch21list05).

##### Listing 21.5. `Person.cs`

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Xml;
using System.Collections;

public class Person {

  private int id;
  private string lastName;
  private string firstName;
  private string userName;
  private string password;
  private string sex;

  public int ID{
    get { return id; }
    set { id = value; }
  }
  public string LastName {
    get { return lastName; }
    set { lastName = value; }
  }
  public string FirstName {
    get { return firstName; }
    set { firstName = value; }
  }
  public string UserName {
    get { return userName; }
    set { userName = value; }
  }
  public string Password {
    get { return password; }
    set { password = value; }
  }
  public string Sex {
    get { return sex; }
    set { sex = value; }
  }

  private ArrayList addresses = new ArrayList();
  public void Add(Address address) {
    addresses.Add(address);
  }
  public ArrayList GetAddresses() {
    return addresses;
  }
  public void Remove(Address address) {
    addresses.Remove(address);
  }
  ArrayList phones = new ArrayList();
  public void AddPhone(ContactInfo phone) {
    phones.Add(phone);
  }
  public ArrayList GetPhones() {
    return phones;
  }
  public void RemovePhone(ContactInfo phone) {
    phones.Remove(phone);
  }
  ArrayList emails = new ArrayList();
  public void AddEmail(ContactInfo email) {
    emails.Add(email);
  }
  public ArrayList GetEmails() {
    return emails;
  }
  public void RemoveEmail(ContactInfo email) {
    emails.Remove(email);
  }

  public override bool Equals(object o){
    Person p = o as Person;
    if (p == null) return false;
    return (p.ID == this.ID);
  }
  public override string ToString(){
    return userName;
  }

  public static ArrayList GetPeople(string filename) {
    ArrayList list = new ArrayList();
    try {
      XmlDocument doc = new XmlDocument();
      doc.Load(filename);
      XmlNodeList persons = doc.GetElementsByTagName
("Person");
      foreach(XmlNode node in persons) {
        Person p = new Person();
        p.FirstName = node.Attributes["firstName"].Value;
        p.LastName = node.Attributes["lastName"].Value;
        p.UserName = node.Attributes["userName"].Value;
        p.Password = node.Attributes["password"].Value;
        p.ID = Int32.Parse(node.Attributes["id"].Value);
        XmlNodeList addresses =
         node.SelectNodes("//Person[@id='"+p.ID+"']/Address");
        foreach (XmlNode address in addresses) {
          Address a = new Address();
          a.Street = address.Attributes["street"].Value;
          a.City = address.Attributes["city"].Value;
          a.State = address.Attributes["state"].Value;
          a.Zip = address.Attributes["zip"].Value;
          a.Country = address.Attributes["country"].Value;
          p.Add(a);
        }
        XmlNodeList phones =
          node.SelectNodes("//Person[@id='"+p.ID+"']/Phone");
        foreach (XmlNode phone in phones) {
          ContactInfo c = new ContactInfo();
          c.Contact = phone.Attributes["number"].Value;
          c.Type= phone.Attributes["type"].Value;
          c.Description= phone.Attributes["description"].
Value;
          p.AddPhone(c);
        }
        XmlNodeList emails =
          node.SelectNodes("//Person[@id='"+p.ID+"']/Email");
        foreach (XmlNode email in emails) {
          ContactInfo c = new ContactInfo();
          c.Contact = email.Attributes["number"].Value;
          c.Type= email.Attributes["type"].Value;
          c.Description= email.Attributes["description"].
Value;
          p.AddEmail(c);
        }
        list.Add(p);
      }
    } catch (Exception e) {
        Console.WriteLine(e.StackTrace);
      }
    return list;
  }
}
```

```
 public class Address {

  private string street;
  private string zip;
  private string city;
  private string state;
  private string country = "USA";

  public string Street {
    get { return street; }
    set { street = value; }
  }
  public string City {
    get { return city; }
    set { city = value; }
  }
  public string State {
    get { return state; }
    set { state = value; }
  }
  public string Zip {
    get { return zip; }
    set { zip = value; }
  }
  public string Country {
    get { return country; }
    set { country = value; }
  }

  public override bool Equals(object o) {
    Address that = o as Address;
    if (that == null) return false;
    return (
      string.Equals(that.Street, this.Street) &&
      string.Equals(that.Zip, this.Zip) &&
      string.Equals(that.Country, this.Country) &&
      string.Equals(that.State, this.State) &&
      string.Equals(that.City, this.City)
    );
  }

  public override string ToString() {
    return "Address with zip "+this.Zip;
  }
}
```

```
 using System.Windows.Forms;
public class PersonNode : TreeNode {

  Person p;
  public PersonNode(Person p) : base (p.ToString()) {
    this.p = p;

  }

  public Person Person {
    get {return p;}
    set {p = value;}
  }

  public override string ToString() {
    return p.ToString();
  }
  public override bool Equals(object o) {
    PersonNode pn = o as PersonNode;
    if (pn == null) return false;
    return (pn.Person.Equals(p));
  }
}
```

### 21.5\. Anchoring and Docking

One of the key differences between the .NET GUI classes and Java AWT and Swing classes is the manner in which they lay out the controls inside a container object. In .NET the default positioning of the controls within the container is absolute. This means that you must specify hard numbers when deciding where exactly to put the control on the container. It also means that the control does not resize when the container is resized. In Java AWT and Swing, the positioning of the controls is relative to the container and is specified using the available layout managers. As a result, the controls resize with the container.

Without code for resizing the controls in .NET, the controls will overlap when the container is resized. The .NET Windows library, however, provides two concepts—anchoring and docking—that allow for the control to be resized automatically with the container.

#### 21.5.1\. Anchoring

When a control is anchored to the edge of the container, the distance between the edge of the control and the edge of the container remains constant when the container is resized. A control can be anchored to any combination of edges, and that causes the control to be resized as needed to maintain the distance between edges. [Listing 21.9](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec5.html_ch21list09) makes this clear.

##### Listing 21.9\. Anchoring a Control

|  
```
 using System;
using System.IO;
using System.Drawing;
using System.Windows.Forms;

public class TestForm : Form {

  Button noResizeButton;
  Button yesResizeButton;
  StreamWriter logger = null;

  public TestForm () {
    noResizeButton = new Button();
    noResizeButton.Text = "Not anchored";
    noResizeButton.Width = 100;
    noResizeButton.Location = new Point(30, 30);

    yesResizeButton= new Button();
    yesResizeButton.Text = "Anchored";
    yesResizeButton.Anchor = AnchorStyles.Left &#124;
                             AnchorStyles.Right &#124;
                             AnchorStyles.Bottom &#124;
                             AnchorStyles.Top;
    yesResizeButton.Width = 100;
    yesResizeButton.Location = new Point(30, 80);
    yesResizeButton.Layout +=
        new LayoutEventHandler(YesLayoutEvent);
    Controls.Add(noResizeButton);
    Controls.Add(yesResizeButton);
    InitLogger();
  }

  private void YesLayoutEvent(object source,
           LayoutEventArgs args) {
    logger.WriteLine("Form.Left - yesResizeButton.Left
        ="+(this.Left-yesResizeButton.Left));
    logger.WriteLine("Form.Right - yesResizeButton.Right
        ="+(this.Right-yesResizeButton.Right));
    logger.WriteLine("Form.Top - yesResizeButton.Top
        ="+(this.Top -yesResizeButton.Top ));
    logger.WriteLine("Form.Bottom - yesResizeButton.Bottom
        ="+(this.Bottom -yesResizeButton.Bottom));
    logger.WriteLine("Form.Left - noResizeButton.Left
        ="+(this.Left-noResizeButton.Left));
    logger.WriteLine("Form.Right - noResizeButton.Right
        ="+(this.Right-noResizeButton.Right));
    logger.WriteLine("Form.Top - noResizeButton.Top
        ="+(this.Top -noResizeButton.Top ));
    logger.WriteLine("Form.Bottom - noResizeButton.Bottom
        ="+(this.Bottom -noResizeButton.Bottom));
  }

  static void Main() {
    Application.Run(new TestForm());
  }

  public void InitLogger() {
    FileStream fs = new
      FileStream("c:\\anchor.txt",FileMode.OpenOrCreate,
      FileAccess.ReadWrite, FileShare.None);
    logger = new StreamWriter(fs);
  }

}
```

 |

[Listing 21.9](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec5.html_ch21list09) is a simple form that contains two button controls. One button is anchored, and the other is not. The two buttons are initialized in the constructor of the form:

```
 noResizeButton = new Button();
noResizeButton.Text = "Not anchored";
noResizeButton.Width = 100;
noResizeButton.Location = new Point(30, 30);

yesResizeButton= new Button();
yesResizeButton.Text = "Anchored";
yesResizeButton.Anchor = AnchorStyles.Left |
                         AnchorStyles.Right |
                         AnchorStyles.Bottom |
                         AnchorStyles.Top;
yesResizeButton.Width = 100;
yesResizeButton.Location = new Point(30, 80);
yesResizeButton.Layout +=
       new LayoutEventHandler(YesLayoutEvent);

Controls.Add(noResizeButton);
Controls.Add(yesResizeButton);
InitLogger();
```

The `yesResizeButton` button is anchored, and this is indicated by specifying the edges to which it is anchored. In [Listing 21.9](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec5.html_ch21list09), this button is anchored to all the edges of the form. This means that the distance between the edges of this button and the form's edges should remain constant as the form is resized.

To show that this is really happening, we record the distance between the edges of the controls and the form in a text file called `anchor.txt`. The `InitLogger` method initializes the file to which this log will be written:

```
 public void InitLogger() {
  FileStream fs = new
    FileStream("c:\\anchor.txt",FileMode.OpenOrCreate,
    FileAccess.ReadWrite, FileShare.None);
  logger = new StreamWriter(fs);
}
```

When the form is resized, the CLR broadcasts events that can be processed by an event handler. The event handler for [Listing 21.9](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec5.html_ch21list09) is specified this way:

```
 yesResizeButton.Layout +=
    new LayoutEventHandler(YesLayoutEvent);
```

In the `YesLayoutEvent` method, we record the distances between the edges of the two buttons and the form. When you run the application and resize the form, the application records every resize event. A sample of the generated text file is as follows:

```

 Form.Right - yesResizeButton.Right =258
   Form.Top - yesResizeButton.Top =8
Form.Bottom - yesResizeButton.Bottom =285

  Form.Left - noResizeButton.Left =58
 Form.Right - noResizeButton.Right =261
   Form.Top - noResizeButton.Top =58
Form.Bottom - noResizeButton.Bottom =335

  Form.Left - yesResizeButton.Left =58
 Form.Right - yesResizeButton.Right =258
   Form.Top - yesResizeButton.Top =8
Form.Bottom - yesResizeButton.Bottom =285

  Form.Left - noResizeButton.Left =58
 Form.Right - noResizeButton.Right =263
   Form.Top - noResizeButton.Top =58
Form.Bottom - noResizeButton.Bottom =334
```

Note that the distance for the anchored control remains the same for all resize events.

#### 21.5.2\. Docking

When a control is docked to an edge of its container, it remains in contact with the edge when the container is resized; the control is resized so that it is the same size as the docked edge. All controls have a `Dock` property, which accepts a value from the `DockStyle` enumeration. The `DockStyle` values are shown in [Table 21.7](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec6.html_ch21table07).

### 21.6\. Drawing with .NET GUI Classes

The drawing classes in .NET are spread throughout a number of namespaces, as listed in [Table 21.8](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec6.html_ch21table08).

Table 21.7\. `DockStyle` Enumeration

| Location | Description |
| --- | --- |

| `Bottom` | The bottom edge of the control is docked to the bottom of the container. |
| `Left` | The left edge of the control is docked to the left of the container. |
| `Right` | The right edge of the control is docked to the right of the container. |

| Namespace | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `System.Drawing` | This namespace provides access to GDI+ basic graphics functionality. The `Graphics` class provides methods for drawing to the display device. The other classes include `Rectangle`, `Point`, `Brush`, `Pen`, and many more. |
| `System.Drawing.Drawing2D` | This namespace provides advanced two-dimensional and vector graphics functionality. |
| `System.Drawing.Imaging` | This namespace provides imaging-related services. |

The features of the .NET GDI+ API are similar to those of the Java 2D API included in the Java platform.

#### 21.6.1. `System.Drawing`

The core class of the `System.Drawing` namespace is the `System.Drawing.Graphics` class, which is similar to the `java.awt.Graphics` and `java .awt.Graphics2D` classes. All the drawing operations are done on the `Graphics` object. To obtain a handle to the `Graphics` object, you can override the `OnPaint` event handler method of the control.

The `Graphics` object is obtained as the property of the `PaintEventArgs` object:

```
 using System.Windows.Forms;
using System.Drawing;

public class DrawingTest : Form {

  protected void OnPaint(PaintEventArgs e) {
    Graphics g = e.Graphics;
  }
}
```

When a component needs to be redrawn manually, the `Paint` event is raised automatically by a call to the `Control.RaisePaintEvent` method. You can also obtain instances of the `Graphics` object by calling the `Control.CreateGraphics` method. When you have a reference to the `Graphics` object, you can use any of its several draw methods to render shapes on the screen. [Table 21.9](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec6.html_ch21table09) lists the methods of the `Graphics` object.

Along with the `Graphics` object, you can use a number of other drawing classes and structs. These are listed in [Table 21.10](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec6.html_ch21table10).

Using these classes and the `Graphics` object, you can commence drawing two- and three-dimensional objects on the screen.

The following code snippets indicate the basic syntax used to achieve some routine drawing tasks. These snippets can be placed in methods of your custom `System.Windows.Form` class. We will use the `CreateGraphics()` method of the `Form` control.

Drawing a Rectangle

```
 Graphics g = CreateGraphics();
Rectangle rect = new Rectangle(50, 30, 100, 100);
Pen pen = Pens.Black;
g.DrawRectangle(pen, rect);
```

Drawing an Ellipse

```
 Graphics g = CreateGraphics();
Rectangle rect = new Rectangle(50, 30, 100, 100);
Pen pen = Pens.Black;
g.DrawEllipse(pen, rect);
```

```
 Graphics g = CreateGraphics();
g.FillRectangle(new SolidBrush(Color.White),
       ClientRectangle);
GraphicsPath path = new GraphicsPath(new Point[] {
  new Point(105, 225), new Point(190, 300),
  new Point(50, 350), new Point(20, 180), },

});
PathGradientBrush pgb = new PathGradientBrush(path);

    Color.Blue, Color.Orange, Color.White,
    };
g.FillPath(pgb, path);
```

#### 21.6.2\. Double Buffering

GDI+ causes the `Graphics` class to update the screen after every drawing operation, and that can cause the screen to flicker. You can eliminate this flicker by using double buffering. In this technique, you execute drawing operations to a `Graphics` object in memory and render the drawing to the screen in a single operation.

You enable double buffering in GDI+ by using the `SetStyle` method of the `System.Windows.Form.Control` class:

```
 SetStyle(ControlStyles.DoubleBuffer, true);
```

Flickering can also occur if the contents of a `Graphics` class are cleared automatically before a component is asked to repaint itself. The following statement can completely eliminate flicker:

```
 SetStyle(ControlStyles.UserPaintControlStyles.AllPaintingIn
Wm|Paint|ControlStyles.DoubleBuffer, true);
```

You can implement double buffering programmatically by executing drawing operations on an in-memory bitmap and then drawing that bitmap in one operation to the `Graphics` object:

```
 Bitmap img = new Bitmap(Width, Height);
Graphics g = Graphics.fromImage(img);
Event.Graphics.DrawImage(img, 0, 0);
img.Dispose();
```

#### 21.6.3\. Sample Drawing Program

[Figure 21.8](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec6.html_ch21fig08) shows a snapshot of what the sample program looks like in action. The program is a trivial shape-drawing application in which a user clicks on the specific shape shown on the toolbar and starts drawing.

##### Figure 21.8\. A Simple GDI+ Drawing Application

![](0672324024_ch21lev1sec6_image01.gif)

One feature of this application is that it allows for the rubber-band effect, which basically stretches the shape in the direction of the mouse movement. When the mouse is released, the shape takes its final form. Although the shape is not actually stretched, the visual effect is achieved by drawing the shape multiple times so that subsequent drawing of the shape undoes the previous drawing.

[Listing 21.10](#0672324024_ch21lev1sec6.html_ch21list10) shows the listing of this example. To keep things focused, the entire application is written in one class.

##### Listing 21.10\. Sample Drawing Application (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Drawing;
using System.Collections;
using System.ComponentModel;
using System.Windows.Forms;
using System.Data;

public class DrawingTest : System.Windows.Forms.Form
{
  private enum Shape {Undefined, Rectangle, Line,
       Circle, Square, Ellipse, Doodle};

  private System.Windows.Forms.ToolBar toolBar;
  private System.Windows.Forms.ToolBarButton rectangle;
  private System.Windows.Forms.ToolBarButton line;
  private System.Windows.Forms.ToolBarButton clear;
  private System.Windows.Forms.ToolBarButton doodle;
  private System.Windows.Forms.ToolBarButton circle;
  private System.ComponentModel.Container components = null;

  private Bitmap bitmap;
  private Shape currentShape;
  private Point previousPoint, currentPoint;
  private int currentWidth, currentHeight;
  private bool dragging = false;
  private System.Windows.Forms.ToolBarButton ellipse;
  private System.Windows.Forms.ToolBarButton square;
  private Graphics gB;

  public DrawingTest() {
    InitializeComponent();
    SetStyle(ControlStyles.UserPaint&#124;
         ControlStyles.AllPaintingInWmPaint&#124;
         ControlStyles.DoubleBuffer, true);
  }

  protected override void Dispose( bool disposing ){
    if( disposing ) {
      if (components != null) {
        components.Dispose();
      }
    }
    base.Dispose( disposing );
  }

  [STAThread]
  static void Main() {
    Application.Run(new DrawingTest());
  }

  private void UnPushAllButtons() {
    foreach (ToolBarButton button in toolBar.Buttons) {
      button.Pushed = false;
    }
  }

  private void toolBar_ButtonClick(object sender,
      System.Windows.Forms.ToolBarButtonClickEventArgs e) {
    UnPushAllButtons();
    ToolBarButton button = e.Button;
    button.Pushed = true;
    switch (button.Text) {
    case "Rectangle":
      currentShape = Shape.Rectangle;
      break;
    case "Line":
      currentShape = Shape.Line;
      break;
    case "Doodle":
      currentShape = Shape.Doodle;
      break;
    case "Circle":
      currentShape = Shape.Circle;
      break;
    case "Ellipse":
      currentShape = Shape.Ellipse;
      break;
    case "Square":
      currentShape = Shape.Square;
      break;
    case "Clear":
      gB.Clear(this.BackColor);
      this.RaisePaintEvent(this, null);
      this.currentShape = Shape.Undefined;
      break;

    }
  }

  private void DrawingTest_MouseDown (object sender,
         System.Windows.Forms.MouseEventArgs e) {
    Point currentPoint = new Point(e.X, e.Y);
    previousPoint = currentPoint;
    dragging = true;
  }

  private void DrawingTest_MouseMove(object sender,
         System.Windows.Forms.MouseEventArgs e) {
    currentPoint = new Point(e.X, e.Y);
    CalculateWidthHeight();
    if (dragging) {
      DrawBackground();
      Pen pen = new Pen(Color.Blue);
      if (currentShape != Shape.Doodle) {
        Graphics g = CreateGraphics();
        DrawShape(pen, g);
        g.Dispose();
      } else {
        DrawShape(pen, gB);
        previousPoint = currentPoint;
      }
      pen.Dispose();
    }
  }

  private void DrawingTest_MouseUp(object sender,
         System.Windows.Forms.MouseEventArgs e) {
    dragging = false;
    CalculateWidthHeight();
    Pen pen = new Pen(Color.Blue);
    DrawShape(pen, gB);
    pen.Dispose();
  }

  private void DrawingTest_Load(object sender,
         System.EventArgs e) {
    Size size =
      SystemInformation.PrimaryMonitorMaximizedWindowSize;
    bitmap = new Bitmap(size.Width, size.Height);
    gB = Graphics.FromImage(bitmap);
    gB.Clear(this.BackColor);
  }

  private void DrawingTest_Paint(object sender,
    System.Windows.Forms.PaintEventArgs e) {
    DrawBackground();
  }

  private void CalculateWidthHeight() {
    currentWidth = currentPoint.X - previousPoint.X;
    currentHeight = currentPoint.Y - previousPoint.Y;
  }

  private void DrawBackground() {
    Graphics gx = CreateGraphics();
    gx.DrawImage(bitmap, 0, 0);
    gx.Dispose();
  }

  private void DrawShape(Pen pen, Graphics g) {
    if (currentShape == Shape.Line) {
      g.DrawLine(pen, previousPoint, currentPoint);
    }
    if (currentShape == Shape.Doodle) {
      g.DrawLine(pen, previousPoint, currentPoint);
    }
    if (currentShape == Shape.Rectangle) {
      g.DrawRectangle(pen, previousPoint.X, previousPoint.Y,
          currentWidth, currentHeight);
    }
    if (currentShape == Shape.Square) {
      g.DrawRectangle(pen, previousPoint.X, previousPoint.Y,
          currentWidth, currentWidth);
    }
    if (currentShape == Shape.Circle) {
      g.DrawEllipse(pen, previousPoint.X, previousPoint.Y,
          currentWidth, currentWidth);
    }
    if (currentShape == Shape.Ellipse) {
      g.DrawEllipse(pen, previousPoint.X, previousPoint.Y,
          currentWidth, currentHeight);
    }
  }
}
```

 |

The entry point of the application is the `Main` method, which instantiates an object of the `DrawingTest` class. The constructor takes the steps necessary to avoid flickering:

```
 SetStyle(ControlStyles.UserPaint|
ControlStyles.AllPaintingInWmPaint|
ControlStyles.DoubleBuffer, true);
```

The toolbar on the top consists of the shapes that can be drawn. The user draws a shape by clicking on any one of the shape buttons. Once pressed, that button stays pressed until another toolbar button is pressed. In this way, the same shape can be drawn multiple times. The Clear toolbar button clears the drawing area.

The drawing action is initiated in the `toolBar_ButtonClick` method, where the `currentShape` of the application is set. The user then uses the mouse to drag the shape. Note that as the user moves the mouse, the shape stretches in the direction of the mouse until the user releases the mouse.

The `DrawingTest_MouseDown`, `DrawingTest_MouseUp`, and `DrawingTest_MouseMove` methods together capture the entire drawing process. In the `DrawingTest_MouseDown` method we set the initial position of the click and set the dragging flag to `true`:

```
 Point currentPoint = new Point(e.X, e.Y);
previousPoint = currentPoint;
dragging = true;
```

To achieve the effect of stretching, you would have to draw multiple shapes of the same type as the mouse moves in such a manner that the next shape drawn undoes the previous one. In the `DrawingTest_MouseMove` method we first obtain the current location of the mouse pointer:

```
 currentPoint = new Point(e.X, e.Y);
```

Then we calculate the distance between the current location and the previously clicked point of the `DrawingTest_MouseDown` method:

```
 CalculateWidthHeight();
```

This basically sets the width as the difference between the X- and Y-coordinates of the two points (the moving `currentPoint` of the `DrawingTest_MouseMove` method, and the fixed `previousPoint` of the `DrawingTest_MouseDown` method). If we are in dragging mode, we undo the previous drawings using the `DrawBackground()` method.

We then set the `Pen` object and draw the appropriate shape in the `DrawShape(pen, g)` method. The `DrawShape` method is where all the drawing takes place.

```
 private void DrawShape(Pen pen, Graphics g) {
  if (currentShape == Shape.Line) {
    g.DrawLine(pen, previousPoint, currentPoint);
  }
  if (currentShape == Shape.Doodle) {
    g.DrawLine(pen, previousPoint, currentPoint);
  }
  if (currentShape == Shape.Rectangle) {
    g.DrawRectangle(pen, previousPoint.X, previousPoint.Y,
           currentWidth, currentHeight);
  }
  if (currentShape == Shape.Square) {
    g.DrawRectangle(pen, previousPoint.X, previousPoint.Y,
           currentWidth, currentWidth);
  }
  if (currentShape == Shape.Circle) {
    g.DrawEllipse(pen, previousPoint.X,
           previousPoint.Y, currentWidth, currentWidth);
  }
  if (currentShape == Shape.Ellipse) {
    g.DrawEllipse(pen, previousPoint.X,
          previousPoint.Y, currentWidth, currentHeight);
  }
}
```

The `DrawingTest_MouseUp` and `DrawingTest_MouseMove` methods call the `DrawShape` method using two different `Graphics` objects. The `Draw ingTest_MouseUp` method uses the `Graphics` object held in memory to render the final shape to the screen. The `DrawingTest_MouseMove` method uses the `Graphics` object obtained by the `CreateGraphics` method. This allows for rapid rendering of the same shape as the mouse moves.

Note that we use programmatic double buffering to create a memory-based `Graphics` object in the `DrawingTest_Load` method and then render everything using this object in the `DrawingTest_Paint` method.

### 21.7\. Summary

GUI programming typically encompasses writing applications with GUI front ends, such as two- and three-dimensional drawing applications, imaging, and printing utilities.

The classes of the `System.Windows.Form` namespace are used for writing applications with a GUI front end consisting of .NET GUI controls. Here are the main points you should remember:

*   The .NET GUI component library closely resembles the Visual Basic world of forms and events. GUI controls are assembled on a form and are connected using events triggered by user actions or by the system. Whereas Java Swing uses the classic model view controller paradigm to separate GUI components from non-GUI components, .NET forms do not provide any logical separation between GUI and non-GUI classes. This might tempt a beginner C# GUI programmer to mix the two types of components, thereby limiting the extensibility and modularity of the GUI application.

*   The Visual Studio .NET environment comes with a Form Designer that makes it trivial to cook up control-rich screens. This is useful for configuring tedious design-time GUI settings. The JDK lacks a built-in GUI designer, and that makes it tedious to rapidly put Swing apps together.

*   The default layout mechanism for the .NET Forms library is absolute positioning of the controls on the form. This means that the controls inside a container do not resize nicely along with the container. To overcome this, .NET introduces the concept of anchoring and docking. In Java AWT and Swing, the positioning of controls inside the container is relative to the container and is done using a suite of layout managers. Therefore, the controls resize automatically with the container without any extra steps.

The .NET GDI+ library allows for complex two-dimensional drawing operations.

*   Much like `java.awt.Graphics` and `java.awt.Graphics2D`, the `System.Drawing.Graphics` object is used for doing all the drawing operations.

*   GDI+ has built-in support for imaging and printing, much like Java's imaging and printing packages.

## Chapter 22\. Reflection

This chapter introduces the classes in C#'s `System.Reflection` namespace. We assume that you are familiar with the general concept of reflection and are somewhat familiar with Java's reflection.

Reflection can be thought of as a “back door” way to get information about objects. In OOP, we can call a method on an object simply by knowing that the method exists on the object. Often, though, when we are dealing with objects in a generic fashion, we do not know about their methods in advance, and sometimes we don't even know the object's type. To call a method on any object without having prior knowledge of the object or its methods, we must query all the methods of the object, find the desired method, and invoke it by passing it parameters at runtime.

To accommodate this, a Java or C# object has associated metadata, or information about its data, such as its fields, its methods, and the constructors and interfaces the object implements. Reflection is the ability to query, search, and use this metadata. Because you must go through the additional step of discovering the method, field, or constructor to call, reflection is always slower than directly calling a specific object method, setting the field, or instantiating the object.

Reflection has a number of important uses:

*   Viewing and querying metadata. Many IDEs use reflection on your custom objects in order to categorize your custom methods and fields in a graphical, treelike format.

*   Dynamic invocation. This allows you to get and set fields of an object at runtime and to invoke methods on that object in a generic fashion. A lot of object-relational tools define mappings from object fields and methods to database table columns. These tools use dynamic invocation to call the appropriate methods to set and get fields on an object after its state is loaded from the database. Java programmers will note that this technique is also used in custom JSP tags.

*   Creating custom types. Java programmers may be familiar with the other two uses of reflection but may be surprised that C# allows you to programmatically access and modify the IL and programmatically create a new type or class. This would be equivalent to two Java APIs: one that allows programmatic access to byte code, and a second one to create classes and interfaces. The core JDK 1.3.1 does not have an API for accessing byte code.

### 22.1\. The Core Reflection Classes

The core classes for reflection in C# are stored in the `System.Reflection` namespace. The close equivalents to those classes in Java can be found in the `java.lang.reflect` and `java.lang` packages.

`System.Type` is the core C# class from which all reflective discovery is done. This class is roughly equivalent to the `java.lang.Class` class. However, there is a difference. In Java, everything is a `java.lang.Object`, so `java.lang.Class` is the metadata of all objects. In C#, `System.Type` can represent any of the following types: classes, value types, arrays, pointers, interfaces, and enumerations. The C# `typeof` operator is somewhat equivalent to the `.class` operator in Java. To get metadata about the `System.String` class, you would use the following:

```
 Console.WriteLine (typeof (System.String).isInterface);
```

This is somewhat similar to the following Java call:

```
 System.out.println ( String.class.isInterface());
```

It is easy to see the members of the `System.Type` class if you are using Visual Studio .NET. The auto-complete feature displays a pop-up box filled with the members. Members of a type include its fields, properties, methods, constructors (which are a special kind of method), custom attributes, interfaces, and any nested types.

[Listing 22.1](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec1.html_ch22list01) browses the members of the `System.Type` class.

##### Listing 22.1\. Members of the `System.Type` Class (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Reflection;

class TypeTest {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    Type t = typeof (System.Type);
    if (!t.IsAbstract) {
      Console.WriteLine("Type has the following constructors");
      PrintConstructors(t);
    }
    PrintMethods(t);
    PrintFields(t);
    PrintProperties(t);
    PrintInterfaces(t);
    PrintAttributes(t);
  }

  private static void PrintConstructors(Type t) {
    Console.WriteLine("This should never get printed ");
  }

  private static void PrintFields(Type t) {
    Console.WriteLine(" $$$$$$ Printing
          fields of the System.Type class ");
    Console.WriteLine(" ");
    FieldInfo[] cons = t.GetFields();
    Console.WriteLine ("There are "+cons.Length+" fields ");
    Console.WriteLine(" ");
    foreach (FieldInfo con in cons) {
      Console.WriteLine ("Field name = "+con.Name);
      Console.WriteLine ("Field Type = "+con.GetType());
      Console.WriteLine ("Is Serialized =
                 "+!con.IsNotSerialized);
      Console.WriteLine ("Is Private = "+con.IsPrivate);
      Console.WriteLine ("Is Static = "+con.IsStatic);
      Console.WriteLine (" ");
    }
  }

  private static void PrintProperties(Type t) {
    Console.WriteLine(" $$$$$$ Printing properties of the
                                      System.Type class ");
    Console.WriteLine(" ");
    PropertyInfo[] cons = t.GetProperties();
    Console.WriteLine ("There are "+cons.Length+" properties ");
    Console.WriteLine(" ");
    foreach (PropertyInfo con in cons) {
      Console.WriteLine ("Property name = "+con.Name);
      Console.WriteLine ("Property Type = "+con.GetType());
      Console.WriteLine ("CanRead = "+con.CanRead);
      Console.WriteLine ("CanWrite = "+con.CanWrite);
      Console.WriteLine (" ");
    }
  }

  private static void PrintInterfaces(Type t) {
    Console.WriteLine(" $$$$$$ Printing interfaces of the
                                      System.Type class ");
    Console.WriteLine(" ");
    Type[] cons = t.GetInterfaces();
    Console.WriteLine ("There are "+cons.Length+" interfaces ");
    Console.WriteLine(" ");
    foreach (Type con in cons) {
      Console.WriteLine ("Interface name = "+con.FullName);
    }
  }

  private static void PrintAttributes(Type t) {
    Console.WriteLine(" $$$$$$ Printing attributes of the
                                      System.Type class ");
    Console.WriteLine(" ");
    object[] cons = t.GetCustomAttributes(true);
    Console.WriteLine ("There are "+cons.Length+" attributes ");
    Console.WriteLine(" ");
    foreach (object con in cons) {
      Console.WriteLine ("Attribute type = "+con.GetType());
    }
  }

  private static void PrintMethods(Type t) {
    Console.WriteLine(" $$$$$$ Printing methods of the
                                      System.Type class ");
    Console.WriteLine(" ");
    MethodInfo[] cons = t.GetMethods();
    Console.WriteLine ("There are "+cons.Length+" methods ");
    Console.WriteLine(" ");
    foreach (MethodInfo con in cons) {
      Console.WriteLine ("Method name = "+con.Name);
      Console.WriteLine ("Is Private = "+con.IsPrivate);
      Console.WriteLine ("Is Static = "+con.IsStatic);
      ParameterInfo[] pinfos = con.GetParameters();
      if (pinfos.Length > 0) Console.WriteLine ("---- Method
                                      parameters-----");
      foreach (ParameterInfo pinfo in pinfos) {
        Console.WriteLine ("Parameter position
                                      ="+pinfo.Position);
        Console.WriteLine ("Parameter name ="+pinfo.Name);
        Console.WriteLine ("Parameter type
                                      ="+pinfo.GetType());
        Console.WriteLine ("In Parameter     ="+pinfo.IsIn);
        Console.WriteLine ("Out Parameter    ="+pinfo.IsOut);
        Console.WriteLine (" ");
      }
      Console.WriteLine (" ============================ ");
      Console.WriteLine (" ");
    }
  }

}
```

 |

Note that `System.Type` is an abstract class and therefore has no constructors. Note also that `printMethods` takes a `Type` parameter. We use the `typeof` operator to get the `Type` object associated with the `System.Class` class.

Because the output of [Listing 22.1](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec1.html_ch22list01) is verbose, we do not list it here; instead, we show the gist of the output in [Table 22.1](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec1.html_ch22table01). The table lists the number of methods, properties, fields, interfaces, and attributes implemented by the `System.Type` class.

In [Listing 22.1](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec1.html_ch22list01), note that `ConstructorInfo`, `PropertyInfo`, `FieldInfo`, `MethodInfo`, and `ParameterInfo` all extend `System.Reflection.MemberInfo.`

Table 22.1\. Metadata Information of the `System.Type` Class

| Item | Count |
| --- | --- |
| Number of methods | 124 |
| Number of properties | 47 |
| Number of fields | 6 |
| Number of interfaces | 2 |
| Number of attributes | 1 |

### 22.2\. Browsing and Querying Members

As you have seen, with 124 methods to browse it can quickly become tedious trying to find the right method with the right signature. Unlike Java, C# provides an API that gives you methods for selecting and searching for a set of members based on certain criteria. The criteria you specify are typically member modifiers that precede the member definition; examples include static, public, and private methods, fields, and constructors.

[Listing 22.2](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec2.html_ch22list02) shows how to browse and query fields and methods of any C# type. The `FindMembers` method of the `MemberInfo` class can be used to narrow the search. The parameters of this method are `MemberTypes`, `BindingFlags`, `MemberFilter`, and `Object.` Let's explore the meanings of these parameters in further detail:

*   `MemberTypes` is an object that indicates the type of the member to search for. These include `All`, `Constructor`, `Custom`, `Event`, `Field`, `Method`, `Nestedtype`, `Property`, and `TypeInfo`. We will also use the `MemberTypes.Method` to find a method. `BindingFlags` is an enumeration that controls the way searches are conducted by reflection. There are a great many `BindingFlag` values, including `IgnoreCase, Instance`, `Public`, `Static`, and so forth. The `BindingFlags` default member indicates no binding flag, which is what we want because we do not want to restrict the binding.

*   `MemberFilter` is a delegate that is used to filter the list of members in the `MemberInfo` array of objects. The filter we'll use is `Type.FilterName`, a field of the `Type` class used for filtering on a name.

*   `Object` is a string value that will be used by the filter. In this case we pass `"Get*"` to match only those methods that begin with the letters `Get`.

##### Listing 22.2\. Browsing and Querying Fields and Methods of a Type (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Reflection;

class FieldTest {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {

    Type t = Type.GetType(args[0]);
    QueryFields(t);
    QueryMethods(t);
  }

  private static void QueryFields(Type t) {
    //Get Fields
    FieldInfo[] f = t.GetFields();
    Display("Get Fields ", f);
    //default fields
    f = t.GetFields(BindingFlags.Default);
    Display("Default ", f);
    //Find all public instance fields
    f = t.GetFields(BindingFlags.Public &#124; BindingFlags.
                        Instance);
    Display("Public and Instance ", f);
    //Find all nonpublic instance fields
    f = t.GetFields(BindingFlags.Instance &#124;
                        BindingFlags.NonPublic);
    Display("Non Public and Instance ", f);
    //Find all public static fields
    f = t.GetFields(BindingFlags.Static &#124;BindingFlags.Public);
    Display("Static and Public ", f);
    //Find all nonpublic static fields
    f = t.GetFields(BindingFlags.Static &#124; BindingFlags.
                        NonPublic);
    Display("Static and NonPublic ", f);
    //Find all public declared-only fields
    f = t.GetFields(BindingFlags.DeclaredOnly &#124;
                               BindingFlags.NonPublic);
    Display("Public and DeclaredOnly ", f);
    //Find all fields
    MemberInfo[] m =
      t.FindMembers(MemberTypes.Field,
        BindingFlags.Default,Type.FilterName, "Get*");
    Display ("Found Field members", m);
  }

  private static void QueryMethods(Type t) {
    //Get Methods
    MethodInfo[] f = t.GetMethods();
    Display("Get Methods ", f);
    //default methods
    f = t.GetMethods(BindingFlags.Default);
    Display("Default ", f);
    //Find all public instance methods
    f = t.GetMethods(BindingFlags.Public &#124; BindingFlags.
                        Instance);
    Display("Public and Instance ", f);
    //Find all nonpublic instance methods
    f = t.GetMethods(BindingFlags.Instance &#124;
                        BindingFlags.NonPublic);
    Display("Non Public and Instance ", f);
    //Find all public static methods
    f = t.GetMethods(BindingFlags.Static &#124; BindingFlags.
                        Public);
    Display("Static and Public ", f);
    //Find all nonpublic static methods
    f = t.GetMethods(BindingFlags.Static &#124; BindingFlags.Non
                        Public);
    Display("Static and NonPublic ", f);
    //Find all public declared only methods
    f = t.GetMethods(BindingFlags.DeclaredOnly &#124;
                               BindingFlags.NonPublic);
    Display("Public and DeclaredOnly ", f);
    //Find all methods
    MemberInfo[] m =
          t.FindMembers(MemberTypes.Method,
            BindingFlags.Default,Type.FilterName, "Get*");
    Display ("Found Method members", m);
  }

  private static void Display(String msg, MemberInfo[] fields) {
    Console.WriteLine ("--------");
    Console.WriteLine (msg);
    Console.WriteLine ("--------");
    foreach (MemberInfo f in fields) {
      Console.WriteLine(f.Name);
    }
  }

}
```

 |

To run [Listing 22.2](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec2.html_ch22list02) we pass a command line parameter:

```
 C:\>Reflection System.Type
```

Here is an excerpt of the output of [Listing 22.2](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec2.html_ch22list02):

```
 --------
Get Fields
--------
FilterAttribute
FilterName
FilterNameIgnoreCase
Missing
Delimiter
EmptyTypes
...
--------
Static and NonPublic
--------
ResolveTypeRelativeTo
ResolveTypeRelativeTo
ResolveTypeRelativeToBaseTypes
--------
```

To print only the name, we treat the `FieldInfo[]` and `MethodInfo[]` collections using the generic `MemberInfo[]`. We can find out the type of the member using the `MemberType` property of the `MemberInfo` class.

[Listing 22.2](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec2.html_ch22list02) deals with fetching a collection of members (fields or methods) either by browsing or calling the `FindMembers` method. Sometimes, though, it is necessary to zoom into a particular method. [Listing 22.3](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec2.html_ch22list03) shows how we can use `GetMethod` to find a particular method. The same calls can be used to get to a specific field, property, or constructor of a type. Using reflection to get a particular member of a type requires knowledge of the existence of that member; otherwise, an exception will occur.

##### Listing 22.3\. Getting Specific Methods of a Type (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Reflection;

class SpecificMethodTest {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {

    Type t = typeof (System.String);
    DoMethod(t);
  }

  private static void DoMethod(Type t) {
    //Getting a method using only the name.
    //This will give an exception
    //Because ToUpper is overloaded. The call below is
    //confusing as to which
    //overloaded method is to be returned.
    MethodInfo m = null;
    try {
      m = t.GetMethod("ToUpper");
    } catch (Exception e) {
      Console.WriteLine(e.Message);
    }
    //Getting a method using only the name. The name
    //is case-sensitive, so the exact name is needed.
    //The method called cannot be overloaded.
    m = t.GetMethod("Remove");
    Console.WriteLine("Default Remove method "  );
    //Getting an overloaded method using the name and the
    //the type of parameters it takes.
    Type[] ta = new Type [] {typeof (int),typeof (char)};
    m = t.GetMethod("PadLeft", ta);
    Console.WriteLine("PadLeft method with params "  );
    //Call a method that takes no parameters
    Type[] noparams = new Type [0];
    m = t.GetMethod("ToUpper", noparams);
    Console.WriteLine("ToUpper method with no params "  );
    //Call a method that takes no parameters
    m = t.GetMethod("Remove", noparams);
    Console.WriteLine("Remove method with no params
                                                  "+(m==null));
  }

}
```

 |

The output of [Listing 22.3](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec2.html_ch22list03) is as follows:

```
 Ambiguous match found.
Default Remove method System.String Remove(Int32, Int32)
PadLeft method with params System.String PadLeft(Int32, Char)
ToUpper method with no params System.String ToUpper()
Remove method with no params True
```

The following excerpt of [Listing 22.3](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec2.html_ch22list03) is particularly interesting. We know that there is only one `Remove` method in the `System.String` class, and it takes two parameters, and we are attempting to get a `Remove` method with no parameters.

```
 //Call a method that takes no parameters
m = t.GetMethod("Remove", noparams);
Console.WriteLine("Remove method with no params "+(m==null));
```

Such a method does not exist in the `System.String` API, and, instead of throwing an exception, the runtime returns a “null” `MethodInfo` object. This can be a little confusing to Java programmers, who expect an exception to be thrown if a method is not found.

Note that in the reflection API, the search and query methods—such as `GetMethod(s)`, `GetConstructor(s)`, `GetMember(s)`, `GetField(s)`, and `GetProperties`—do not throw a `NoSuchMemberException` or a derivative; instead, they return a `null` object if the member is not found or defined for that type. This approach is somewhat different from that of the Java world, where a checked exception (`java.lang.NoSuchMethodException` or `java.lang.NoSuchFieldException`) gets thrown when a member (field, method, or constructor) cannot be found for a particular class. We will leave it to the language gurus to debate which is philosophically more sound: returning `null` or throwing an exception. Java programmers who are used to using exceptions for control flow should be aware of this subtle difference in C#.

### 22.3\. Invoking Methods and Setting Fields and Properties

So far we have seen how to query, search, and retrieve specific type members or a collection of type members. The true power of reflection lies in invoking those methods and constructors and setting those properties and fields. [Listing 22.4](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec3.html_ch22list04) shows invoke operations on the `System.String` class.

##### Listing 22.4\. Invoke Operations Using Reflection (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Reflection;

class InvocationTest {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {

    Type t = typeof (System.String);
    CallConstructor(t);
    CallMethod(t);
    GetProperty(t);
  }

  private static void CallConstructor(Type t) {
    //Tried to get the default no-args public constructor.
    // String s = new String(char[] c);
    ConstructorInfo constructor =null;
    constructor = t.GetConstructor(new Type[] {typeof
                                                    (Char[])});
    Char[] carr = new Char[] { 's', 'u', 'g', 'a', 'r' };
    object[] args = new object[1] {carr} ;
    try {
      Console.WriteLine(constructor.Invoke(args));
    } catch (Exception e) {
      Console.WriteLine(e.StackTrace);
    }
  }

  private static void CallMethod(Type t) {
    MethodInfo method =null;
    String target = "sugarless";
    method = t.GetMethod("Remove");
    object[] args = new object[] {5,4};
    Console.WriteLine(method.Invoke(target, args));
  }

  private static void GetProperty(Type t) {
    PropertyInfo property = null;
    property = t.GetProperty("Length");
    String args = "floccinaucinihipilification";
    Console.WriteLine(property.GetValue(args, null));
  }
}
```

 |

The output of [Listing 22.4](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec3.html_ch22list04) is as follows:

```
 sugar
sugar
27
```

To truly appreciate the power of reflection, we will write a utility that lets us query in-memory collections. The `System.Collections` classes (see [Chapter 14](#0672324024_ch14.html_ch14)) are type-agnostic, so they can be used to hold objects of any type. Using reflection, we can ask for objects from a collection meeting specific criteria. For simplicity we assume that it is a homogeneous collection (one that contains only one type of an object). [Listing 22.5](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec3.html_ch22list05) shows a sample class whose objects we will store in the collection.

##### Listing 22.5\. The `Person` Class (C#)

|  
```
 using System.Text;

public class Person {

  private string firstname;
  private string lastname;
  private int age;
  private float salary;
  private bool male;

  public Person (string fname, string lname,
             int age, float salary, bool male) {
    this.firstname = fname;
    this.lastname = lname;
    this.age = age;
    this.salary = salary;
    this.male = male;
  }

  public override string ToString() {
    StringBuilder builder = new StringBuilder();

      builder.Append(firstname+","+lastname+",
                       "+age+","+salary+","  ale);
    return builder.ToString();
  }
}
```

 |

The basic idea behind the `QueryList` collection is to be able to query objects from it that meet specific criteria. For example, if we were to store only `Person` objects in the list, then we could ask for `Person`s meeting specific criteria (for example, all persons with `firstname` Jack, all persons with `salary` > $60000, all males under 40 years of age). [Listing 22.6](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec3.html_ch22list06) shows the bulk of the `QueryList` class.

##### Listing 22.6\. The `QueryList` Class (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Collections;
using System.Reflection;
using System.Text;
public class QueryList : ArrayList {

public enum Operation : int {
    OBJECT_EQUALS = 1,
    PRIMITIVE_EQUALS,
    LESS_THAN_OR_EQUAL,
    GREATER_THAN_OR_EQUAL,
    LESS_THAN,
    GREATER_THAN,
    NOT_EQUALS
  }

  public QueryList() : base() {
  }
  public QueryList(ICollection coll): base(coll) {
  }
  public QueryList(int size): base(size) {
  }

  public QueryList GetList(string field, int val,
                         Operation operation) {
    return _GetList(field, val, operation);
  }
  public QueryList GetList(string field, bool val,
                         Operation operation) {
    return _GetList(field, val, operation);
  }
  public QueryList GetList(string field, float val,
                                Operation operation) {
    return _GetList(field, val, operation);
  }
  public QueryList GetList(string field, string val,
                                Operation operation) {
    return _GetList(field, val, operation);
  }
  public QueryList GetList(string field, int val) {
    return _GetList(field, val, Operation.PRIMITIVE_EQUALS);
  }
  public QueryList GetList(string field, bool val) {
    return _GetList(field, val, Operation.OBJECT_EQUALS);
  }
  public QueryList GetList(string field, float val ) {
    return _GetList(field, val, Operation.PRIMITIVE_EQUALS);
  }
  public QueryList GetList(string field, string val) {
    return _GetList(field, val, Operation.OBJECT_EQUALS);
  }
  private QueryList _GetList(string field, object val,
                                       Operation oper) {
    QueryList list = new QueryList();
    IEnumerator myEnumerator = GetEnumerator();
    while (myEnumerator.MoveNext()) {
      object o = myEnumerator.Current;
      Type t = o.GetType();
      FieldInfo info = t.GetField(field, BindingFlags.Public &#124;
          BindingFlags.NonPublic &#124; BindingFlags.Instance );
      object targetval = info.GetValue(o);
      switch ((int)oper) {
        case (int)Operation.OBJECT_EQUALS: if
          (val.Equals(targetval)) list.Add(o); break;
        case (int)Operation.PRIMITIVE_EQUALS : if
          (val == targetval) list.Add(o); break;
        case (int)Operation.GREATER_THAN : if
          (!_IsBool(targetval.GetType()) &&
          _GetDouble(targetval)
          > _GetDouble(val)) list.Add(o); break;
        case (int)Operation.LESS_THAN : if
          (!_IsBool(targetval.GetType()) &&
          _GetDouble(targetval) < _GetDouble(val))list.Add(o);
                                     break;
        case (int)Operation.LESS_THAN_OR_EQUAL : if
          (!_IsBool(targetval.GetType()) &&
          _GetDouble(targetval) <=
          _GetDouble(val)) list.Add(o); break;
        case (int)Operation.GREATER_THAN_OR_EQUAL : if
          (!_IsBool(targetval.GetType()) &&
          _GetDouble(targetval) >=
          _GetDouble(val)) list.Add(o); break;
      }
    }
    return list;
  }

  private bool _IsBool(Type t) {
    return t.Equals(typeof (bool));
  }

  private double _GetDouble(object o) {
    return Double.Parse(o.ToString());
  }

public override string ToString() {
  StringBuilder sbf = new StringBuilder();
  IEnumerator myEnumerator = GetEnumerator();
  while (myEnumerator.MoveNext()) {
    sbf.Append(myEnumerator.Current.ToString()).Append("\n");
  }
  return sbf.ToString();
}
}
```

 |

The class `QueryList` extends `ArrayList.` The API for this class contains overloaded methods for searching the collection. The general signature of the calls is as follows:

```
 GetList ( String field, String value)
GetList ( String field, int value)
GetList ( String field, float value)
GetList ( String field, bool value)
```

Basically, we want to search for those objects in the collection whose field name `"field"` has the value specified in the value argument. This call can be used to search for simple criteria. The following code gets all persons with the first name of Jack:

```
 GetList ("firstname", "jack")
```

There is a three-argument call that looks like this:

```
 GetList ( String field, int value, Operation oper)
GetList ( String field, float value, Operation oper)
```

where `Operation` is a public enumeration indicating the various operations supported.

So a criterion such as all persons with salary > 60000 would be expressed as follows:

```
 GetList ("salary", 60000, QueryList.Operation.GREATER_THAN);
```

Note that the `GetList` method returns a `QueryList`. This means that we can chain method calls and thereby combine criteria. So to get all males under age 40, we would first find all males and then, within that set, find those under the age 40:

```
 GetList ("male", true).GetList ("age", 40,
QueryList.Operation.LESS_THAN);
```

This may not be the most efficient way to handle a query. However, the purpose of this exercise is to show how reflection can make it possible to write generic utilities.

[Listing 22.7](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec3.html_ch22list07) shows the driver class that uses the `QueryList` object.

##### Listing 22.7\. Driver Class for Executing the `QueryList` Utility (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
class QueryListDriver {
  public static void Main(string[] args) {

    QueryList list = new QueryList();
    list.Add( new Person("jack", "daniel",26, 60000, true));
    list.Add( new Person("bud", "weiser",33, 75000, true));
    list.Add( new Person("jack", "monroe",40, 150000, false));
    list.Add( new Person("jack", "kennedy",38, 100000, false));
    list.Add( new Person("ozzy", "ozbourne",50, 200000, true));
    list.Add( new Person("pat", "boone", 70, 40000, true));
    list.Add( new Person("bill", "gates", 45, 900000000,
                                                        true));
    list.Add( new Person("lady", "diana", 36, 80000, false));

    Console.WriteLine("All people with firstname \"jack\"");
    Console.WriteLine(list.GetList("firstname","jack"));

    Console.WriteLine("All people with salary > 60000 ");
    Console.WriteLine(list.GetList("salary",60000,
             QueryList.Operation.GREATER_THAN));
    Console.WriteLine("All males less than 40 yrs of age ");
    Console.WriteLine(list.GetList("male",true).GetList("age",
                        40, QueryList.Operation.LESS_THAN));
  }
}
```

 |

The output of [Listing 22.7](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec3.html_ch22list07) is as follows:

```
 All people with firstname "jack"
jack,daniel,26,60000,True
jack,monroe,40,150000,False
jack,kennedy,38,100000,False

All people with salary > 60000
bud,weiser,33,75000,True
jack,monroe,40,150000,False
jack,kennedy,38,100000,False
ozzy,ozbourne,50,200000,True
bill,gates,45,9E+08,True
lady,diana,36,80000,False

All males less than 40 yrs of age
jack,daniel,26,60000,True
bud,weiser,33,75000,True
```

You can use the `QueryList` class when you are populating an `ArrayList` with objects from a database and do not want to go back to the database to get a different view of the same list or a subset of the list. For example, if the `Person` class were mapped to a database row, fetching all the `Person` objects at once and then using the `QueryList` class would eliminate the need to run different select queries based on the criteria being used.

### 22.4\. Generating Dynamic IL Using Reflection Emit

In Java it is possible to generate source code dynamically and compile it to byte code. In fact, the JSP technology is based on just that principle, in which the JSP is compiled at runtime to a servlet class, which is then run by the JVM.

In C#, too, you can generate the code and compile it at runtime. However, C# goes a step further and provides an API for actually dealing with the generated IL, a capability known as reflection emit. This would be equivalent to a Java API that manipulates byte code. The classes in the C# `System.Reflection.Emit` namespace can be used to programmatically generate IL instructions.

To better understand what we mean by this, let's look at a simple example. [Listing 22.8](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec4.html_ch22list08) is a simple class that basically generates the number 3 on the system console when run. Here we actually wrote the `SimpleClass` class in our IDE, compiled it, and ran it.

##### Listing 22.8\. A Simple Class (C#)

|  
```
 using System;

public interface ISimple {
  int GetInt();
}

public class SimpleClass : ISimple {
  public int GetInt() {
    return 3;
  }
  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    ISimple sc = new SimpleClass();
    Console.WriteLine(sc.GetInt());
  }
}
```

 |

It is possible to achieve the same result as that of [Listing 22.8](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec4.html_ch22list08) by defining `SimpleClass` programmatically instead of writing it. [Listing 22.9](#0672324024_ch22lev1sec4.html_ch22list09) shows the code for doing that.

##### Listing 22.9. Programmatic Generation of `SimpleClass` Using Reflection Emit (C#)

|  
```
 using System;
using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Reflection;
using System.Threading;
using System.Reflection.Emit;

public class Driver {
  public interface ISimple {
    int GetInt();
  }

  public static void Main(string[] args) {

    AssemblyName assemblyName = new AssemblyName( );
    assemblyName.Name = "GeneralAssembly";
    AssemblyBuilder newAssembly =
      Thread.GetDomain().DefineDynamicAssembly(
      assemblyName, AssemblyBuilderAccess.Run);
    ModuleBuilder newModule =
      newAssembly.DefineDynamicModule("Simple");

    TypeBuilder myType =
      newModule.DefineType(
      "SimpleClass", TypeAttributes.Public);

    myType.AddInterfaceImplementation(
      typeof(ISimple));

    Type[] paramTypes = new Type[0];
    Type returnType = typeof(int);
    MethodBuilder simpleMethod =
      myType.DefineMethod(
      "GetInt",
      MethodAttributes.Public &#124;
      MethodAttributes.Virtual,
      returnType,
      paramTypes);
    ILGenerator generator =
      simpleMethod.GetILGenerator( );

    generator.Emit(OpCodes.Ldc_I4, 3);
    generator.Emit(OpCodes.Ret);

    MethodInfo getIntInfo =
      typeof(ISimple).GetMethod("GetInt");

    myType.DefineMethodOverride(simpleMethod, getIntInfo);
    myType.CreateType( );
    ISimple sc =
```
